name: Animal Charity Evaluators (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each animal charity it reaches, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: Animal Charity Evaluators evaluates animal advocacy charities, recommends the most effective, and passes donors' money to them through its Recommended Charity Fund and to small groups through its Movement Grants; this model covers all its own spending in its year to March 2025 ($1.72M; the $4.6M of grants it passed on are the recipients' cost). By its own surveys, with unrecorded gifts and our non-response step, it caused about $5.7M of giving to animal charities that year, three dollars per dollar it spends, valued at its Recommended Charities' figures on this site (ACE's own evaluations of them) weighted by its fund's split, shifted money only for its gain over an ordinary animal charity, and the next dollar at 30% of the past average: about 0.0000071 years of healthy life per $1,000 at the site's animal weights. The result moves most with the animal weights and its next-dollar figure; no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

name: Animal Policy International: welfare standards for imported animal products (charityevals, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a net harm at the defaults, so by where its result falls: the compliance costs of the import rules on shoppers, by branch (EU 51%, UK 39%, New Zealand 10%); the EU's part spread over its five most populous members by population, a stand-in for the whole union. The animals spared are abroad (mostly in Ukraine and Türkiye for the EU branch).
summary: Animal Policy International, founded in 2023 through Ambitious Impact's incubation programme, researches and campaigns for rules that imported eggs and pork meet the welfare standards of the country importing them, in the EU, the UK and New Zealand. No such rule has been won yet, so this model counts what its 2025 work (a declared budget of €120,000 for its EU entity, about $180,000 for the whole organisation by our judgment) adds to the chance of three: cage-free requirements for the EU's egg imports (40% chance; about 9.3 million caged hens abroad supply them), a UK requirement on pork from sow stalls and New Zealand's bans on sow stalls and battery cages applied to imports, each at API's share of the advocates and 2025's share of its work. The hens and sows spared are counted in the shared suffering figures, and the dearer eggs and pork as a compliance cost. At the site's default weight of a chicken's pain against a person's, the shoppers' cost (for the EU, API's own estimate of the rise in egg prices, on the value of EU egg production) outweighs the hens' and sows' gain, so the result is a net harm, about 0.0 years of healthy life per $1,000; it turns positive only with chickens weighed about two hundred times higher. Both sides are mostly the EU branch and mostly judgment: the chance the EU rule passes, how many hens actually leave cages rather than the trade shifting, and API's small part in a crowded EU field; every branch is discounted for missing data, and the next dollar counts at 57% of the average.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Animal Policy International: welfare standards for imported animal products (charityevals, 2025)

name: ASPCA: farm animals
beneficiaries_note: Our build: US hens and sows under state laws and higher-welfare purchases.
summary: The ASPCA's farm animal welfare team, a small part of its $422m spending in 2025 (about $8m with its share of public education, our judgment), lobbied against federal and state rollbacks of the laws that keep hens out of cages and sows out of crates, and pushed shoppers, farmers and producers toward higher-welfare products and in-ovo sexed eggs. Defending the laws also keeps their compliance costs (the regulator's figure for California's Proposition 12, about $300 million a year net of retailers' margin), which at the site's values outweigh the animals' gain, so the result is below zero in expectation, about −0.0004 years of healthy life per $1,000. Both are small per dollar: the defence is shared with a coalition in which the ASPCA's own spending (about $1.5m of lobbying and outreach) is a small part, its 2025 work removed only a share of the override risk, and its large reserves make the next dollar worth less than the average. The biggest uncertainties are that cost, the share of the risk the opposition removed, how many hens and sows would go back into cages if the laws fell, the coalition's total spending and the share of the ASPCA's policy spending that goes on farm animals, which the accounts don't give; the result is mostly uncertainty, spanning several orders of magnitude, and both branches are discounted for missing outcome data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: ASPCA farm animal welfare (defending state cage and crate laws, higher-welfare market work, 2025)

name: ASPCA
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the ASPCA works only in the United States (owners and their dogs, cats and horses).
summary: The ASPCA, the oldest US animal welfare charity, placed about 70,900 animals in homes in 2025 (including relocation from crowded shelters), treated 109,700 animals in its hospital and low-cost clinics, supported 129,200 spay/neuter surgeries, ran Animal Poison Control, rescued animals from disasters and cruelty cases, gave $29m in grants to shelters, trained vets and shelter staff, ran national adoption campaigns and won puppy-mill laws; this model covers all of that except its farm-animal work, which has its own model. At the site's defaults it comes to about 0.00014 years of healthy life per $1,000: care for one dog or cat at a time reaches few animals per dollar, and nearly all of the result is the life satisfaction of owners whose pets the low-cost clinics treat, feed or keep at home. The biggest uncertainty is that owners' gain and how much suffering each kind of care spares an animal, all our judgment, so the result is mostly uncertainty, spanning about three orders of magnitude; every branch is discounted for missing outcome data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: ASPCA (shelters, veterinary care, neutering, cruelty and disaster response, grants, education and policy for dogs, cats and horses, 2025)

name: Dogs Trust
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. people in the UK (behaviour-line owners, Freedom's survivors and their children, homeless owners: about 84%) and UK and Irish dogs (under 1%); fewer dog bites and overseas treatment, neutering and training (about 15%) spread over WVS's and the grantees' main countries by grant size (a judgment).
summary: Dogs Trust, the UK's largest dog welfare charity, rehomed about 10,000 dogs in the UK and Ireland in 2025, ran a behaviour support line and other prevention services, fostered dogs for people escaping domestic abuse, campaigned for the 2025 law against puppy smuggling, and through its sister charity Worldwide Veterinary Service treated and sterilised dogs overseas; this model covers all of that except rabies vaccination, which has its own model. At the site's defaults it comes to about 0.000053 years of healthy life per $1,000 because care for individual dogs reaches few animals per dollar: about $205m for a few hundred thousand days of a dog's disabling pain spared, most of them from neutering and treatment overseas, and at the default weight on animal suffering the dogs' days count less than the people the work also helps: owners given behaviour advice, survivors of domestic abuse (and their children) who could leave because Freedom kept their dog, and homeless owners (together most of the result, judgments), and fewer people bitten where neutering shrinks free-roaming populations (a side effect). The biggest uncertainties are the people's gains, how much a rehomed or neutered dog's life improves (our judgment, with no study measuring it), and the weight on animal suffering; every branch is discounted for missing data, and the model's own ranges together span more than a thousandfold, so the figure is mostly uncertainty.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Dogs Trust (rehoming, prevention, international dog welfare and campaigns, 2025)

beneficiaries_note: Our build: animals, by share of the result at the defaults. A judgment.
summary: The Humane League's other programmes cost about $5.2 million in 2025, its programme spending less its grants and its accountability campaigns (two other lines): defending US state cage-free and crate-free laws against a federal override and supporting the Animal Policy Alliance's local campaigns, winning new corporate cage-free commitments (four companies, 1.6 million hens), running the Open Wing Alliance (its team, summits, trainings and Fair and Fowl report, credited with a share of the members' 216 new cage-free policies, 16 restored pledges and 18 broiler policies abroad), and mobilising volunteers and supporters to press companies to keep their commitments (a share of the 5.5 million hens out of cages at companies THL pressed itself). summary: ALLFED (the Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters) researches foods and food systems that could feed people after a catastrophe that blocks the sun or breaks the food supply, chiefly the famine after a nuclear war's soot cools the climate, and advises governments on plans for it; this model covers all its programmes in 2024 ($1.0M spent). The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts those deaths: Rethink calls its figures placeholders, the range runs ten times either way, and they were not set with food resilience in mind; the result also moves with the years a cut counts and the discount rate. Both branches, nuclear winter and pandemics, are discounted for missing data: no food plan has been tested in a catastrophe.

name: Coalition for Rainforest Nations (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the forest's carbon, the buyers' extra emissions and the pandemic risk forest loss carries all reach the whole world, spread by world population.
summary: The Coalition for Rainforest Nations helps rainforest countries in the UN climate talks, trains their teams to measure and report their forest results so they can be paid for cutting deforestation, and helps them sell forest carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. We model all of its 2024 programme spending ($4.0 million) in three branches: the forest kept by donors' results-based payments; the forest kept by credit sales, less the extra emissions of buyers who count the credits against their own targets; and the climate-finance goal agreed at COP29, its adaptation money valued as aid and its mitigation money in tonnes. The result is a small net harm, close to zero, and nearly all of it is the finance goal: some climate finance is aid moved from health, education and other development work into mitigation, which is worth far less in healthy years, and at the best guesses the aid lost slightly outweighs the new adaptation aid and the mitigation gained, with its cleaner air. The share of the goal's money that is new aid decides the sign: at about half new the result is zero, and above it positive. The forest branches rest on one evaluation, Norway's payments to Guyana, credit CfRN with its small share of all the money behind the forest kept, and are small; the credit sales are a small net harm. Every branch takes the missing-data discount, and the result is mostly uncertainty: in the simulation it is harmful in about three draws of five.

rows.explainer: Everything the Coalition for Rainforest Nations (CfRN) spent on its one reported programme in 2024, the latest year filed: REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation), its "ongoing flagship program" (Part III). The return says the statements were not audited or reviewed by an accountant (Part XII line 2), so the Form 990 is the accounts. Its 2024 Annual Impact Statement describes three pillars inside that programme: the UN climate negotiations, national implementation (carbon-market laws, registries and sales) and data collection and capacity building. All three are modelled below, as three branches: forest kept by donors' results-based payments, forest kept by credit sales under Article 6 net of buyers' extra emissions, and the climate-finance goal (rbf_share_of_programme, fin_share_of_programme).

rows.explainer: Contractors who train government forestry teams as staff would (Convention 1 counts them with staff). The other professional fees ($1,336,316: legal, registry and communications work) are left out: firms paid market rates, with no forgone pay.

rows.label: Share of the programme on measuring forest results for results-based payments
rows.explainer: CfRN reports no split of its one programme. Our judgment: 45% (30-60%) goes to work that lets rainforest countries measure, report and have verified their forest results and claim results-based payments from donors (the rbf branch): training and data collection with 15 countries in 2024 (forest reference levels, greenhouse-gas inventories, biennial reports; the forestry experts' $631,375 in Schedule O) and the negotiations on REDD+ finance. A tenth goes to the climate-finance goal (fin_share_of_programme). The rest goes to the carbon markets of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (the itmo branch): negotiating its rules, completed at COP29 in 2024, and national implementation in four countries (carbon-market laws, registries, readying Suriname's credits for sale), which the 2024 Impact Statement gives as much space. Anchor: the statement's own weight among its pillars; travel and meetings ($522,448) serve all three.

rows.label: Share of the programme on the negotiations for the climate-finance goal
rows.explainer: The finance goal was one of the two COP29 results CfRN's Impact Statement leads with, but one strand of its negotiations work beside REDD+ and Article 6, which take its data, legal and implementation teams. Our judgment a tenth (3-20%) of the programme.

Climate-finance goal agreed at COP29: a year by 2035

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: all countries had agreed to triple climate finance for developing countries from $100 to $300 billion annually by 2035

rows.explainer: The new collective quantified goal: developed countries to provide or mobilise $300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035.

rows.label: The $100 billion goal it replaces

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: all countries had agreed to triple climate finance for developing countries from $100 to $300 billion annually by 2035

rows.explainer: The goal set in 2009 for 2020, which the new goal triples.

rows.label: Share of the rise in climate finance that the goal itself causes
rows.explainer: Climate finance was rising before the goal and would go on rising with development banks' plans and donors' budgets; a goal adds pressure and a yardstick, but nothing binds a donor. Anchor: the $100 billion goal, due by 2020, was reached only in 2022, two years late, at $115.9 billion (OECD, reported by Clean Energy Wire), so goals of this kind are met late and largely by finance that was coming anyway. Our judgment: 15% of the $200 billion rise is the goal's own doing (3-40%). Whether it is delivered at all is fin_implementation_adj; whether the goal itself would have been agreed anyway is fin_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Share of the goal's finance worth as much as a grant
rows.explainer: The goal counts loans at face value and private money mobilised; a loan repaid is worth only its subsidy to the borrower, and a project financed by a market-rate loan would often have been financed anyway. Anchor: of the $115.9 billion of 2022, "most of it is provided as loans" (Oxfam's Jan Kowalzig, in Clean Energy Wire's report of OECD's figures). Our judgment 40% (20-70%), the grant-equivalent part. Applied to both the aid's value and the mitigation tonnes: only the subsidy decides whether a project happens.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the money for adaptation and cross-cutting aid
rows.explainer: In 2022 "less than one third" of climate finance went to adapting to climate change and "most" to mitigation (OECD, reported by Clean Energy Wire); cross-cutting projects (both at once) are valued with adaptation as aid. Our judgment 35% (25-50%). The rest, mitigation, is counted in tonnes (fin_mitigation_tco2e_per_year), as the site counts every mitigation (docs/normalization.md 2.20: aid whose use is known is valued at that use's figure).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the money that is new aid, not diverted from other aid
rows.explainer: Much public climate finance is development aid relabelled or moved from health, education and other aid. CARE's Seeing Double (2023, p. 4): "only 7 per cent of the climate finance provided from 2011 to 2020 is found to be new and additional" to donors' aid commitments, and under the weak definition 52% is development finance diverted (https://care.dk/media/ckjh2s3p/seeing-double-2023.pdf). Our judgment 40% new (7-70%), between Seeing Double's two definitions. The diverted money loses the value of the aid it replaced (docs/normalization.md 2.20: aid displaced counts).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of a dollar of aid
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure for a donor's aid budget (docs/normalization.md 2.20), for the adaptation aid gained and the other aid displaced alike.

rows.label: Value lost per dollar of rich donor countries' public money, units of value
rows.explainer: What a dollar of a donor government's money costs its taxpayers (docs/normalization.md 2.23): the shared cost of raising public funds (facts: public_funds.mcpf) over taxpayers' consumption on the survey scale, at the site's European figure (UK consumption per person × its survey ratio, 2.14) for the donors (Norway, Germany, the Green Climate Fund's contributors, Japan, Switzerland), with the US federal payer multiple as the shared stand-in for how a national tax falls (our judgment: no other country's figure is shared yet).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: prices in 2035 against 2024
rows.explainer: The goal is in dollars of the day, not indexed, and the model counts in 2024 dollars (Convention 8). Anchor: the Federal Reserve's and the ECB's 2% inflation targets over eleven years, 1.02^11 = 1.24 (1.15-1.40). No shared inflation forecast exists in facts/.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: grant-equivalent finance it adds a year at the 2035 level, in 2024 dollars
Climate-finance goal: share of the money that isn't new whose use is unchanged (rebadged)
rows.explainer: Money that fails CARE's test of new aid isn't all aid moved to new uses: CARE calls much of it development finance "rebadged" with climate objectives (Seeing Double 2023, p. 7), and its p. 6 cites studies finding that donors over-report the climate relevance of their projects. Rebadged money neither loses an aid project nor builds a mitigation project: its value is zero. Our judgment 40% (20-70%) of the money that isn't new.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value as aid a year, net of the aid displaced and of what the new money costs its payers
rows.formula: fin_grant_dollars_per_year * fin_value_per_dollar * (fin_adaptation_share * fin_new_aid_share - (1 - fin_adaptation_share) * (1 - fin_new_aid_share) * (1 - fin_rebadged_share)) - fin_grant_dollars_per_year * fin_new_aid_share * donor_payer_uov_per_dollar
rows.explainer: New money for adaptation adds the value of aid; money moved to adaptation from other aid nets to nothing (aid for aid); money moved to mitigation loses the aid it replaced, and its tonnes are counted separately; rebadged money changes nothing. Negative when the money moved to mitigation outweighs the new adaptation money. New money also costs the donors' taxpayers (row donor_payer_uov_per_dollar, docs/normalization.md 2.23); money moved from other aid costs them nothing more.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: grant-equivalent finance per tonne of CO₂e its mitigation projects avoid over their lives
rows.explainer: Anchor on the row's own basis: the Green Climate Fund's 286 projects "are expected to abate a total of 3.1 billion tonnes" over their lives, and its allocation "stands in grant equivalent terms at ... 44 per cent (USD 4.3 billion) for mitigation" (GCF report to COP29, UNFCCC FCCC/CP/2024/3, p. 3, https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cp2024_03a01.pdf): about $1.4 a tonne of grant-equivalent GCF money, about $3.4 with the co-financing counted at a quarter of its face value. Those are the accredited entities' own ex-ante estimates; projections of this kind run ahead of what is built and claim cuts that would have come anyway (families/climate.md), so our judgment is about three times the ex-ante figure (the $3.4 counts the $45.6 billion of co-financing at a quarter, split like GCF money with 54% to mitigation: $4.3 billion + 0.54 × 0.25 × $45.6 billion ≈ $10.5 billion over 3.1 billion tonnes; the haircut is our judgment, not a published evaluation), $10 ($3-40, from no haircut to ten times).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: CO₂e its added mitigation finance avoids over the projects' lives, per year of finance at the 2035 level
rows.explainer: New and moved mitigation money alike build projects; rebadged money builds nothing new.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years over which a mitigation project's tonnes come
rows.explainer: The cost per tonne buys a project's lifetime tonnes, which come over its years of use and are discounted (the climate family's direct cuts). Anchor: energy access and power generation take "the largest portion of GCF funding (39 per cent)" of its mitigation (GCF report, p. 3); power plants and grids run 20-30 years, efficiency and transport projects less. 20 years (10-30).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: air pollution its mitigation tonnes carry, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Anchor: energy and power take about two fifths of mitigation finance (GCF report, p. 3: 39%), and low-emission transport much of the rest; in developing countries the power displaced is largely coal and diesel without scrubbers, whose smoke per tonne is at or above the world fossil average the shared rate is built on; forests and farming carry no fuel smoke. Our judgment half the world fossil-fuel average (10-120%).

rows.explainer: Grants for the kind of work CfRN does: helping countries build forest monitoring, reference levels and REDD+ strategies.

rows.label: Years the assessment's totals cover

source.title: Forest Declaration Assessment (February 2022), Reward results by countries and jurisdictions
source.quote: Since 2010, approximately USD 24.5 billion – an average of USD 2.4 billion per year – has been channeled

rows.explainer: The assessment's own average: $24.5 billion at $2.4 billion a year is about ten years, 2010 to about 2020 (published February 2022). It cancels out of the result (rbp_per_year scales the tonnes and CfRN's share alike).

rows.label: Results-based payments a year, all REDD+ countries
rows.explainer: About $460 million a year. Commitments, not disbursements: some is paid years later or never (the shortfall sits in rbp_evidence_adj; the attribution row divides by commitments too).

rows.label: Readiness and implementation support per dollar of results-based payments
rows.explainer: Grants for the kind of work CfRN does (forest monitoring, reference levels, REDD+ strategies) over the payments for results: about $0.39 of support per dollar paid. The base of CfRN's share in both forest branches: the payers and the forest countries' own budgets, which carry out the protection, are under the mobiliser's share.

rows.label: Carbon markets: money paid a year for rainforest countries' forest credits under Article 6, once the market works
rows.explainer: No forest credit had been transferred under Article 6 by the end of 2024: Suriname announced the world's first sale of such credits (Impact Statement 2024, p. 4) and expected it in 2025. Anchors: Hess's purchase of Guyana's jurisdictional credits, at least $750 million over 2022-2032, about $75 million a year for one country; all donors' results-based payments, about $460 million a year. Our judgment: $200 million a year ($50 million to $1 billion). It cancels out of the result: CfRN's share of the resources falls as the market grows (itmo_attribution_share).

rows.label: Carbon markets: price of a forest credit (a tonne of reduced emissions)

source.title: Stabroek News (11 January 2023), Hess makes US$75M first payment for Guyana-issued carbon credits
source.quote: US$37.5 million for 2.5 million ART-TREES credits from 2016 at a price of US$15/tonne of CO2e

rows.explainer: Hess's deal with Guyana, the largest sale of a country's forest credits so far, is worth at least $750 million between 2022 and 2032; its first payment priced the 2016 and 2017 credits at $15 a tonne, and later vintages are priced higher. Our estimate $15 ($10-30), the quoted price: $10 is the low end of jurisdictional forest credits, $30 a price only the best-rated units reach.

rows.label: Carbon markets: forest credits sold a year
Tropical forest in the countries working under the UN's REDD+ framework

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: around 90% of the world’s tropical forests and span an area of about 1.6 billion hectares

rows.explainer: Context only, not on the path to the result: the forest the payments and credit sales below can reward (read by tco2e_per_hectare_year): the model counts tonnes from dollars, not from hectares, because neither CfRN nor its partner countries publish the forest their finance keeps. The hectares kept a year are rbf_ha_per_year and itmo_ha_per_year.

rows.label: Health: people with fewer illnesses from the forest kept
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Livelihoods: people whose income changes
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Wellbeing: people whose life satisfaction rises from nature kept
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: animal-years affected
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, Guyana 2010-2015 (dollars of the time)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: Based on assumed payments of US$250 million, the cost of the 12.8 million tons of avoided CO2 emissions is US$19.53 per ton of CO2.

rows.explainer: The one quasi-experimental evaluation of a national results-based REDD+ programme: Norway's offer of $250 million to Guyana for keeping deforestation low in 2010-2015 cut tree-cover loss by 35% against a synthetic control, 12.8 million tonnes of CO₂, $19.53 a tonne if the loss avoided is permanent (that question is permanence_share). The paper reports bootstrapped 95% intervals only in its appendix; the range, $12 to $40, is ours, wider on the high side because Guyana's reference level was set high and other countries' programmes may buy less.

rows.label: Years of the Norway-Guyana payments (2010-2015)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: with Norway offering to pay US$250 million to Guyana if annual deforestation rates remained below 0.056% from 2010 to 2015.

rows.explainer: Six years, 2010 to 2015: the payments' price level is the average of those years'.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, in 2024 dollars
rows.explainer: Guyana's cost per tonne in 2024 prices (× US consumer prices in 2024 over their 2010-2015 average, about 1.36: Convention 8), so that it divides 2024 dollars of payments, credit sales and CfRN's spending alike: about $26.65.

rows.label: Share of the forest kept that stays standing for good
rows.explainer: Tree-cover loss in Guyana rose after the payments ended (Roopsind et al. 2019: "without continued payments, forest protection is not guaranteed"), so some forest kept is only cleared later. Our judgment half (20-90%).

rows.label: Share of the clearing avoided that moves elsewhere
rows.explainer: A country paid to clear less may push clearing (gold mining, farming, logging) across the border; Roopsind et al. flag leakage as possible but unmeasured. Our judgment 20% (0-50%), as for the leakage rows of The Nature Conservancy's forest branches. Failure of the main effect, so it stays in the main chain, not among side effects.

rows.label: How far Guyana's result holds for the payments CfRN's countries get
rows.explainer: Guyana's is one country, with low deforestation and a forward-looking contract that rewarded each year's restraint. Most of the money CfRN helps countries claim pays for results years after the fact (Honduras's 2016-2020 results were verified in 2024), which rewards the past more than it changes the future, and reference levels set high pay for reductions that would have come anyway. Our judgment 0.5 (0.2-1), anchored on The Nature Conservancy's 0.4-0.75 for forest rules judged from other places' studies. Used for both branches' forest tonnes.

rows.label: CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost
rows.explainer: The tropics' average, 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares lost in 2023 (about {{row:tco2_per_ha_lost}} tonnes a hectare; World Resources Institute, the shared figures every forest model reads). Only used to turn tonnes into hectares for the pandemic-risk rows.

rows.label: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all the finance, per hectare of REDD+ forest
rows.explainer: For reading only: the forest carbon the donors' payments and the credit sales keep a year (before CfRN's share), spread over the 1.6 billion hectares under REDD+. Nothing on the path reads it.

rows.label: Years of forest kept that a year's work counts
rows.explainer: One, for the two forest branches (the finance goal counts its own won years, fin_years): both set a year of CfRN's spending against a year of the finance flows it shares in, with CfRN credited its share of that year's resources (an ongoing flow counts one year against one year's cost, Convention 3). The new Article 6 rules are part of the stock of rules and institutions every year's flow rests on, which is why the flow, not the rule, is counted.

rows.label: Years from the year's work until the forest is kept
rows.explainer: Countries CfRN helps report in one year and are paid a year or more later (Honduras's results verified in 2024, its first sales planned for 2025); Article 6's first forest credits were due on the market in 2025-2027. The forest kept follows the expectation of payment, so about two years (half a year to four). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years of forest kept, discounted
Results-based finance: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all donors' payments, for good
rows.explainer: The year's payments over the cost per tonne, × the share that stays standing, × the share not displaced. How far Guyana's result holds is the branch's evidence adjustment.

rows.label: Results-based finance: CO₂ kept, discounted years
Results-based finance: tropical forest kept a year
Carbon markets: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by the money buyers pay
rows.explainer: The same chain as results-based payments: money paid for results keeps forest standing at Guyana's cost per tonne, × permanence, × leakage, × how far Guyana's result holds (applied here, not in the branch's evidence row, so it doesn't shrink the buyers' extra emissions below as well).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of the credits bought by countries for their own targets
rows.explainer: Article 6 credits go to countries counting them against their national pledges (Switzerland, Sweden, Japan, Singapore's government), to airlines under CORSIA, to companies under carbon taxes that accept them (Singapore's), and to companies buying voluntarily (CfRN's REDD.plus platform). CfRN's own plan is purchases "by corporations and sovereign governments", possibly through a carbon tax like Singapore's (Impact Statement 2024, p. 32). Our judgment: half to countries (20-80%).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of countries' credits that replace cuts they would otherwise make
rows.explainer: A country that counts a forest credit against its own target can cut a tonne less at home. If the credit is a real extra tonne kept, the two cancel; if not, the world emits more. The real tonnes are itmo_forest_tco2e_per_year; this row is how many of countries' credits replace cuts they would otherwise have made. A country that would have met its target anyway replaces cuts one for one; one that would have missed it (CfRN: the credits "help developed countries who fail to hit their climate pledges") replaces fewer. Our judgment half (20-90%). The failure of the market's main chain (credits for reductions that would have happened anyway), so it is in the main chain, not a side effect.

rows.label: Carbon markets: real cuts in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought
rows.explainer: An airline under CORSIA or a company buying voluntarily would otherwise have bought another credit; a company under a carbon tax would otherwise have paid the tax. So a forest credit they buy instead loses only the real cut in the unit it displaced, and none where the tax would have been paid. A blend: Probst et al. (2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11564741/) estimate that "less than 16%" of credits issued are real cuts (25% for avoided deforestation), an upper bound, × the three quarters of these buyers we judge buy instead of another credit rather than instead of a tax. 12% (0-30%), no fuel smoke: the displaced units are mostly other offsets.

rows.label: Carbon markets: extra fossil emissions by country buyers a year
Carbon markets: extra emissions a year from all buyers
rows.explainer: Countries' forgone cuts at home, plus the real cuts lost in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought.

rows.label: Carbon markets: CO₂ kept a year, net of buyers' extra emissions
rows.explainer: Negative when the buyers' extra emissions exceed the real tonnes the money keeps: at the best guesses each credit sold at $15 keeps about a tenth of a tonne of forest carbon (Probst et al. 2024 find a quarter of avoided-deforestation credits real, a cross-check) and lets buyers emit about three tenths of a tonne more.

rows.label: Carbon markets: net CO₂, discounted years
Carbon markets: tropical forest kept a year
Catastrophic risk: deaths if the catastrophe happens
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance below is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about {{row:pandemic_annual_probability}} a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drove
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than {{row:land_use_share_of_emergence}} of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (facts/catastrophe.json): half of the land-use risk scales with tropical forest loss (10-100%), anchored on Allen et al. (2017). No study has measured this dose.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance per hectare of tropical forest kept
rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept. The least grounded number here.

rows.label: Results-based finance: fall in the yearly pandemic chance × discounted years
Carbon markets: fall in the yearly pandemic chance × discounted years
rows.explainer: From the forest kept only; the buyers' extra emissions clear no forest.

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: mostly older people died, few young children.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: school-age children were the least affected.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: about 15% of adult excess deaths were under 50; the rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number.

rows.label: Results-based finance: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value
Results-based finance: what the donors' payments cost their taxpayers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: Public money that buys tonnes is netted against what it costs those who pay for it (docs/normalization.md 2.23): the year's payments × the value lost per dollar, over the same discounted years as the forest kept; credited with the branch (in uov_bridged), all but its evidence step, which is about the tonnes.

rows.label: Carbon markets: what governments' purchases of credits cost their taxpayers, units of value (negative)
rows.explainer: The credits bought by countries for their own targets are bought with public money (docs/normalization.md 2.23); companies' purchases are their own money, as any private purchase. Over the same discounted years as the forest kept, credited with the branch.

rows.label: Carbon markets: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value
Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance from the year's work
rows.explainer: For reading: the forest each branch keeps × its credit × the risk per hectare.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the win due to all its advocates
rows.explainer: The goal is agreed, so the chance is the shared share of a won climate policy due to all advocates together, rather than to governments, events and opinion (facts/climate.json, {{row:fin_p_success}}, 10-60%); CfRN's part of the advocates is fin_attribution_share.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years of negotiation behind it
rows.explainer: The talks on the new goal ran from the decision at COP26 (2021) to its adoption at COP29 (2024), about three years (2-5). As a past average, a year's spending gets one year's share of the win (Convention 11).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years until the added finance flows at the goal's level
rows.explainer: The goal's level is "by 2035", eleven years after 2024; the money counted is that level, so the wait is to 2035 (8-14: some of it sooner, some later than the goal). Discounted at the shared rate (normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The site's years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted, normalization.md 2.9), after the wait, discounted.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of the finance added, one year's share of the win
rows.explainer: The value of the finance the goal adds a year, net of aid displaced, × the advocates' share of the win × the discounted years counted ÷ the years of negotiation. Compliance costs (normalization.md 2.21): none counted beyond the aid displaced, since the goal binds no payer and new aid is valued as aid won is everywhere on the site.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: mitigation tonnes, one year's share of the win, before waits and years counted
rows.explainer: Used to weight the smoke these tonnes carry (air_pollution_weight), which may read no shared value.

The donors who pay and the governments that do the protecting are under the mobiliser's share, not in this denominator. Measured over all REDD+ countries, which scales the tonnes alike.

rows.explainer: A new goal was due anyway: the Paris decision (1/CP.21, para. 53) required one before 2025 "from a floor of USD 100 billion per year", and the COP29 presidency's draft of 22 November 2024 already proposed $250 billion a year, raised to $300 billion the next day (UN News, 22 November 2024, https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/11/1157346). Our judgment: half the rise from $100 billion to $300 billion wasn't coming anyway (25%, only the last step from the draft, to 80%). Whether the finance follows the goal is fin_added_by_goal_share; the advocates' part of what was won is fin_p_success.

Our judgment, a rough count without a published tally: about 50 groups at $0.5-3 million a year each on this item, about $80 million, with a wide range ($20-300 million) because the count is ours. name: Cool Earth (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. The cash's value to the communities (97%) split by note 8's programme spending (Peru 76%, Papua New Guinea 16%, Cameroon 6%; the small grant to Go Conscious Earth spread pro rata); the forest's carbon and pandemic risk (3%) spread by world population.
summary: Cool Earth funds Indigenous and local communities in Peru, Papua New Guinea and Cameroon to keep their rainforest standing, mostly with cash given directly to households and community committees, plus data, training and fire prevention. We model all of its programme spending in the year to 31 January 2026 ($4.3 million) in two branches: the forest the support keeps from clearing (a small cut in pandemic risk, and its carbon), and the value of the cash (about £1.2 million) to the people who get it. The result is about 0.11 years of healthy life per $1,000: over nine tenths of it is the cash itself, valued like a cash transfer to some of the poorest people in Peru and Papua New Guinea. The forest's part is small and rests on a judgment of how much clearing the support prevents; both branches take the missing-data discount, since neither is measured against a comparison.

name: Earthjustice: biodiversity (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the counted good is forest carbon kept out of the air, which spares people everywhere (heat deaths).
summary: Earthjustice's species, public-lands and oceans work (our judgment: 30% of its programme spending, $41.2M in the year to June 2025). The one win of fiscal 2022-2025 we can put on the site's scale is the Tongass National Forest's roadless protection, restored in January 2023 on 9.37 million acres after tribes and groups represented by Earthjustice sued, counted for the forest carbon logging would have released; the species wins (gray wolves relisted, other Endangered Species Act protections, a marine monument kept closed to fishing) count nothing, since whether more wild animals alive is a gain is unknown. At the defaults it comes to about 3.4e-7 years of healthy life per $1,000 because the Forest Service expected the 2020 exemption to change overall logging little, so the restored protection spares only about a hundred hectares a year of 3.8 million, much of that timber is cut elsewhere instead, and the protection is again under threat. The biggest uncertainties are how much logging the 2020 exemption would have brought, the years counted and the discount rate; the branch is discounted for missing data.

name: Earthjustice: climate and clean energy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population; the small US coal-smoke share is left in the world figure.
summary: Earthjustice (San Francisco), the largest US non-profit environmental law firm, litigates and advocates on climate and clean energy, healthy communities and biodiversity; this model is its climate and clean-energy work (our judgment: 45% of programme spending, $61.8M of the $137.4M it spent itself in the year to June 2025, after $16.8M of donated legal work and advertising). It counts three wins of fiscal 2022-2025 we can put tonnes on: EPA's 2023 oil and gas methane rule and 2024 power-plant carbon standards (at the shared tonnes, status and credit steps for each rule) and the US coal plants that closed in 2022-2025, of which advocacy is credited with 15% and Earthjustice with a tenth of that, plus 50% for its many state and other wins. The households the law's subsidies tipped into switching lose a little on it before the subsidy (our guess, −$120 a year each), which alone puts the tonnes' part slightly below zero. The biggest uncertainties are the shared missing-data step, advocacy's share of a won policy, the next-dollar figure and Rewiring America's share of the advocacy behind the rebates; since May 2026 the rebates no longer pay for switching from gas, so less of them will be paid. summary: SilverLining (Washington, DC) funds and coordinates research on solar radiation modification (cooling the planet by reflecting a little sunlight) and works with governments and others on how it is researched and governed; this model values what it added to that field in 2019-2024: its own research grants and science, its engagement work and grants abroad, other funders' money it directed, and the US federal research line (NOAA's Earth's Radiation Budget, about $8M a year since 2020) its policy work helped start, against its spending over those years ($6.5M in 2024). A dollar of the field's work is worth a share of the heat deaths a use of cooling would avert, put into tonnes of CO₂ by how much a tonne warms: a 30% chance of a use this century, 0.6°C for 50 years, the field's work adding a tenth of its benefit by improving how it is used, over all the field's funding until then. At the defaults a dollar given averts the heat deaths of about 0.3 tonnes of CO₂, about 0.060 years of healthy life per $1,000; cooling acts on the warming itself, so the decision the field informs weighs hundreds of billions of tonnes, and the field is small (about $44M a year). Whether cooling is used at all is one event, so at the default risk setting the counted figure is near zero. The result is mostly uncertainty, resting on judgments no study settles (how much the field's work improves a use, whether there is one), and every branch is discounted for missing data.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: from the model's rows at the defaults, about seven tenths of the value is money for power customers where reactors are built (China about 60%, other countries about 33%, India about 7%), the rest the tonnes (heat deaths world-wide, air pollution by coal capacity times smoke per tonne: China and India).
summary: TerraPraxis, a US non-profit with a small UK sister company, designs, convenes and builds software to re-power the world's coal plants with advanced nuclear reactors (its REPOWER consortium), and makes the case for advanced nuclear more broadly (the Ten-Terawatt Initiative). This model counts what its 2022-2024 work ($6.3M) adds to a yardstick, a third of the COP28 pledge to triple nuclear capacity, read at about 2040 (the middle of the years counted), a tenth of it on coal sites, crediting all groups' non-commercial enabling work with 1.5% of that deployment and TerraPraxis with 8% of that work on coal sites and 0.6% elsewhere. Besides the tonnes, the deployment changes what people pay for power: reactors on coal sites are cheaper to build (DOE: 15%-35%), while at the site's discount rate new reactors' power costs about as much as the coal and gas it replaces and, in India, more than the wind and solar it replaces (IEA/NEA projections, with wind and solar's system costs); since most reactors would be built in China and other middle-income countries, where a dollar is worth far more to those paying it, the coal sites' construction savings outweigh the tonnes (in India they are largely offset by nuclear's cost over the wind and solar it replaces). At the defaults a dollar given comes to 0.0045 years of healthy life per $1,000, about seven tenths of it from those savings. It is mostly uncertainty: nothing has been built yet, every step from the work to a reactor is a judgment, and the sign turns on what nuclear power will cost against what it replaces; both lines are discounted for missing data.

name: The Nature Conservancy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. PRANA's crop-burning deaths in northwest India (48%); forest and land carbon, power displaced and pandemic risk, spread by world population (41%); adaptation's coastal people in Mexico and Hawai'i (6%, split by judgment); the fisheries rules' fishers in the Seychelles and the Pacific islands (3%, split by judgment); the year's deals' local incomes in Ecuador and The Bahamas (2%, by their people).
summary: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) buys and protects land and water in the US and about 80 countries, brokers debt-for-nature deals with governments, and works on clean energy, food systems, fresh water and fisheries. We model all of its fiscal year 2025 spending (July 2024 to June 2025, $1.28 billion of conservation programmes and land purchases), each of its nine pathways from the research on its kind of work, in 13 branches: forest kept by the Ecuador Amazon deal, the land it bought and its protection policy; power displaced by mine-land solar and renewable siting maps; Pará's deforestation-free cattle rule, zero-conversion soy in the Gran Chaco, regenerative farming and the PRANA no-burn programme in India; restoration; fisheries rules; and climate adaptation. The result is about 0.00023 years of healthy life per $1,000, because most of TNC's work keeps land carbon, which is worth little in healthy years, and TNC is a small share of the resources behind its large deals, rules and policies. Nearly half of it is the air-pollution deaths averted by less crop burning in Punjab and Haryana, most of whose fall would have come anyway; a third is the Pará cattle rule, mostly through the least grounded step, a small cut in pandemic risk from forest kept, and its roll-out has barely begun. Every branch rests on thin data and is discounted for missing data, and the result is mostly uncertainty (plausible range 0.000075 – 0.00075).

name: Union of Concerned Scientists: climate, transport and western states (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults. The public money the Inflation Reduction Act won for US households (18.5%) is in the United States; the tonnes (81.5%) spare people everywhere, spread by world population, the small US power-plant and vehicle smoke share left in the world figure.
summary: The Union of Concerned Scientists' climate and clean energy, clean transportation and western states programmes ($32.8M with overhead in the year to September 2025) do technical analysis and advocacy for US climate policy; this model counts the five largest policies it worked on that were won in October 2021 to September 2025 with published tonnes (the Inflation Reduction Act, EPA's 2024 vehicle and power-plant standards, California's Advanced Clean Cars II rule and its 2025 extension of its carbon market to 2045), with its other state clean-energy laws and its climate-accountability science as a share. At the defaults that is a small net harm, −0.00045 years of healthy life per $1,000: a dollar given averts about 0.0053 tonnes of CO₂e (about $190 a tonne), but the act, which gives about three fifths of the gross tonnes, buys them with public money (about $65 billion a year) that costs taxpayers more than the tonnes are worth on the site's scale; the public money it won for households' home rebates and credits and the won rules' compliance costs are counted too; each win is shared with many groups and with what governments would have done anyway (UCS is credited with 1% to 10% of the advocacy behind each), and the federal rules and the law's credits have since been repealed or cut back and California's car rule has lost its federal waiver. The biggest uncertainties are the discount rate, the shared years a won reform counts and the deaths per tonne; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no tonne is measured for its work.

name: Union of Concerned Scientists: food and farms (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the flood protection kept is for households in the US Upper Midwest.
summary: The Union of Concerned Scientists' Food and Environment programme ($4.5M in the year to September 2025, $5.1M with overhead) does analysis and advocacy on farms and food: wetlands and the farm bill's conservation rules, fertilizer, groundwater, farm trade and farmworkers. This model counts its one win of the year with a value at stake: its estimate that the Upper Midwest's wetlands avert about $23 billion of flood damage a year was part of the case for the federal wetland protections (Swampbuster) that a court upheld in May 2025 against a challenge filed in 2024; its other work is a share. At the defaults a dollar given keeps about 0.00014 years of healthy life per $1,000 in expectation (flood damage averted, valued as consumption to the average American), from 0.0 to 0.0024 on its plausible range. It is low because the challenge was unlikely to succeed, the government and four other groups fought the case (UCS, not a party, is credited with 1%), only farmed wetlands are at stake and drain slowly, and the money kept goes to US households, where a dollar does far less than in poor countries. The result is mostly uncertainty: the share credited to UCS, the chance the challenge would have won and the drainage rate each move it several times. The one branch is discounted for missing data: nothing about the work's outcome is measured.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Union of Concerned Scientists (food and farms)

name: Action for Happiness: wellbeing courses and digital programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build, weighted by branch result: the courses and groups (about 15%) 80% in the UK (343 of the first 431 courses, Krekel et al. 2021) and the rest elsewhere, and the digital programme (about 85%), an English-language online audience, judged at 40% UK, 25% US, 6% each Canada and Australia, 3% Ireland and 20% elsewhere.
summary: Action for Happiness, a UK charity, spent £551,000 in 2025 on 160 volunteer-led Happiness Habits wellbeing courses (about 1,900 people), 115 volunteer-led local groups, and a digital programme (calendars of daily actions, an app, the 10 Days of Happiness emails and live talks) through which it says 190,000 people took at least one wellbeing action. The courses' effect blends the randomised trial of their predecessor, Exploring What Matters (life satisfaction up 0.63 standard deviations, about a point), with the literature on group positive psychology courses; the digital programme takes the literature on self-help exercises for the share of people judged to use a programme like the trials' (15%). The digital programme's reach is an audience built since 2011 and served at mostly fixed cost, so its result is a past average and counts at the charity's next-dollar figure (44%); the courses are priced per course. It comes to about 0.12 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.032 – 0.44), about 85% of it from the digital programme. Every branch is discounted for missing data (no trial of today's six-week course, the local groups or the digital programmes); the biggest uncertainties are how many of the 190,000 get anything like a programme and how long the effects last.

name: All Hands and Hearts: schools and relief abroad (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the Myanmar earthquake response and school rebuilds in Nepal, the Philippines and Mexico: shares of the result at the defaults.
summary: All Hands and Hearts' work abroad in the year to August 2025 (the latest audited year; its Afghanistan and Gaza responses began after it): the Myanmar earthquake response through local partners (cash, water, shelter materials and hygiene supplies, then a water and hygiene programme in 12 villages: 13,000 people), and school rebuilds for disaster-hit communities (Bandevi School in Nepal, two bamboo-frame schools in the Philippines and 17 classrooms repaired in Oaxaca, Mexico). Its accounts don't split spending by country, so the $2.0 million modelled here is our judgment of the share abroad (18%, from 10% to 30%), which moves the result in proportion. The relief is valued as goods at their cost on the site's log-income scale at the affected households' consumption, plus the few excess deaths clean water and shelter avert; each school as its building's cost spread over its pupils and years, for the years it brought forward. The result, about 0.087 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.015 to 0.5); three-quarters of it is the Myanmar relief, valued at a judged $40 a person. Both branches are discounted for missing data: the counts are All Hands and Hearts' own and what each person got is a judgment. The biggest uncertainties are the share of spending abroad, the value of the relief per person and what others would have done anyway.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: All Hands and Hearts' school rebuilds and disaster relief abroad (year to August 2025)

name: All Hands and Hearts (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: US disaster response (muck and gut, mould sanitation, smoke remediation) and home repairs.
summary: All Hands and Hearts sends volunteers, led by its own staff, to US disasters to muck and gut flooded homes, sanitise them against mould, clean smoke-damaged houses after the Los Angeles fires and repair homes; its school rebuilds and relief abroad are a model of their own. The US work is modelled for the year to August 2025, the latest audited year: $9.2 million of its $11.2 million of cash programme spending (the split with the work abroad is our judgment, since the accounts give none), for about 800 muck and guts, 370 mould sanitations, 170 smoke-cleaned homes and an estimated 90 homes repaired, each valued at what a contractor would charge, on the site's log-income scale at the clients' consumption, with the volunteers' own wellbeing as a side effect (2%). The result, about 0.0025 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.0006 to 0.014), is low because the help goes to US households, whose consumption the site's log-income scale makes a dollar do little for, and because the volunteers' unpaid time (about 190,000 hours) and donated materials are much of what the work takes, so All Hands and Hearts' cash is credited with about half of it. Every branch is discounted for missing data: the counts are rounded, the homes repaired are our estimate and the value of the work to those served is a judgment. The biggest uncertainties are that value and what others would have done for the households anyway.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: All Hands and Hearts' US disaster response and home repairs (year to August 2025)

name: ARMoR (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the deaths new antibiotics reach, 55% in high-income countries (the model's access_hic_share) spread over the largest by their resistance deaths, the rest over the countries with most resistance deaths (GRAM 2021), each weighted by access: a judgment, as no source splits the deaths reached by country.
summary: ARMoR (the Alliance for Reducing Microbial Resistance) argues in Europe for paying drug makers for new antibiotics through subscriptions, so that new drugs get developed although they are kept in reserve. We count its spending from its launch in September 2023 to December 2025 against what it won: a voluntary framework for member states' joint subscriptions in the EU pharmaceutical package agreed in December 2025, which it had made its key ask, at a 5% share of the campaigners' credit. If member states fund it, the extra antibiotics avert deaths from drug-resistant infections, mostly of older people, less what the payments cost those who pay. At the defaults it comes to about 0.0 years of healthy life per $1,000; the result is mostly uncertainty: whether member states ever fund the framework, how many drugs a reward brings and ARMoR's share of the credit are all judgments. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and its national advocacy and paid research won no change in the period, so they count as cost only.

summary: Ambitious Impact (formerly Charity Entrepreneurship) researches intervention ideas and founds new charities to run the best of them; this model covers all its programmes in the year to March 2025: the nine charities and five effective giving organisations it launched, Founding to Give, its funding circles, grantmaker and research training, and its research, against its own spending of $2.5M (the seed grants it passed on are valued as money for the new charities). At the defaults it averts about 6.5 years of healthy life per $1,000: each charity founded is credited with the average lifetime fundraising of its charities ($107M raised by 60 so far, times 2.5 for the years to come), 60% of it caused by Ambitious Impact, valued at the figures the rankings give the charities it has launched, institutional funders' grants as all shifted and the rest half new money, each effective giving organisation and Founding to Give company with the donations it is expected to move, at GiveWell's Top Charities, less the giving organisations' running costs, the giving organisations' part at Ambitious Impact's share of the credit (50%; the organisation that asks the donor takes the rest); the next dollar at 36% of the past average. It creates charities that each go on to raise and spend several times its cost per charity, most of them in global health. The result moves most with the missing-data discount, where shifted money would otherwise have gone, the discount rate and the next-dollar figure; the projected part of its charities' future fundraising, the giving organisations' and companies' donations, the spending its grantmaker training and research changed and its fellows' careers are discounted for missing data.

name: American Cancer Society: Hope Lodge, rides to treatment and the helpline (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Hope Lodge lodging, Road To Recovery rides and the helpline and information for patients in the US.
summary: The American Cancer Society's patient services in the US, year to March 2026: free lodging at its Hope Lodge communities (565,000 nights), Road To Recovery volunteer rides to treatment (93,000 rides for 7,500 patients) and its 24/7 helpline (284,000 calls, chats, emails and texts) with online information and peer support, about $235m of its $426m patient-support line (the rest, prevention and screening promotion, is in the research-and-policy model). Lodging and rides are valued as money saved, on the site's log scale for patients' households, plus a small judged chance that they keep a patient's treatment on track; information and support as a small, short wellbeing gain scaled down from trials of psychosocial support for people with cancer. The result, about 0.0036 years of healthy life per $1,000, is low because a few thousand dollars saved is a small gain to a US household and a call is a small dose of support; every branch is discounted for missing data, since ACS counts nights, rides and contacts but measures no outcomes. How often lodging and rides keep treatment on track and how much a call or a page helps are the biggest uncertainties, and the result is mostly uncertainty.

name: American Cancer Society: research, advocacy and screening promotion (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's cancer burden (28% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population), ACS CAN's US policy wins and US screening promotion (72%).
summary: The American Cancer Society funds cancer research ($193m in the year to March 2026: 934 active grants at 219 institutions and its own population and statistics research), campaigns through its advocacy affiliate ACS CAN ($55m: tobacco taxes, insurance coverage of screening and testing, cancer-research budgets), and promotes screening and prevention (about 45% of its $426m patient-support line, a judgment). Research is valued as ACS's share (about 0.25%, drug companies' research included) of the world cancer burden a year of the field's research averts sooner; tobacco advocacy as ACS CAN's share of the US smoking burden a typical year's US tobacco wins avert (the site's shared tobacco figures), coverage advocacy as its share of the US cancer burden the year's coverage and budget wins avert; screening as ACS's share of the year's gain in US screening; the deaths inside every branch's DALYs are valued by age. The result, about 0.0022 years of healthy life per $1,000, is low because research results arrive after about 15 years and are shared with a field spending about $70bn a year, policy and screening gains are shared with many groups and fall mostly on people over 50, and a past average counts at the next dollar's share (46%); all three branches are discounted for missing data, since ACS measures no health outcome of its own spending. It is dominated by judgment (the share of the burden the year's policy wins avert, the share of the burden a year of research averts, ACS's shares of the credit), so the result is mostly uncertainty; Hope Lodge, rides to treatment and the helpline are the separate patient-services model.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: American Cancer Society: research, advocacy and screening promotion (charityevals, 2025-26)

name: American Red Cross: blood supply and lifesaving training (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US blood supply and US training courses.
summary: The American Red Cross collects about 40% of the US blood supply (6.4 million blood products to some 2,500 hospitals in FY2025, the latest audited year) and trains about 6 million people a year in CPR, first aid and water safety. Hospitals and course fees pay for both, and more than their cost (biomedical revenue $2.31 billion against $2.12 billion of expenses; programme-materials (mainly course) revenue $175 million against $143 million), so this model has weight 0 in what a donation to the Red Cross does; it shows what the work itself achieves per dollar spent on it, in years of healthy life per $1,000. Both branches are discounted for missing data: the deaths averted per blood product rest on judgments anchored on studies of patients who refused transfusion, and the training on registry studies of bystander CPR. The biggest uncertainty is the counterfactual: other US blood centres and course providers would supply most of it if the Red Cross didn't. Four steps shrink the result: other providers would step in (20% of a year's outcome counted), the Red Cross's product is about a third of the resources behind each transfusion, both branches take the missing-data step, and a transfusion survivor lives about three-fifths of an average remaining life. Together the adjustments leave about 3% of the raw outcome; before them a death averted costs about $25,000 of blood. The judgments behind deaths averted per product span a wide range, so the result is mostly uncertainty.

summary: The Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids campaigns for tobacco-control laws: in ten low- and middle-income priority countries and Africa ($29.5m in the year to March 2025, much of it paid for by Bloomberg Philanthropies' restricted grants), in the US ($8.4m: taxes, flavour rules, FDA regulation) and, through its Global Health Advocacy Incubator ($6.1m), on food, road safety and other health policy. Each branch is CTFK's share of the people and money behind a typical recent year's wins (15% in the US, 25% in the priority countries) times the share of the smoking or diet burden those wins avert (0.25% a year of the priority countries' smoking burden), anchored on estimates of what the world's tobacco-control policies of 2007–2020 achieved; deaths are valued by age, half the cut in smoking pays off after about 8 years (quitters) and half after about 40 (young people who never start), the site's shared tobacco figures, and second-hand smoke is counted as a side effect. The result, about 0.063 years of healthy life per $1,000, rests on tobacco killing about 1.6 million people a year in the priority countries and a won tax or law lasting; it is dominated by judgment (the share of the burden a year's wins avert and CTFK's credit for them), all three branches are discounted for missing data, since no change in smoking from CTFK's own wins is measured, and the next dollar counts at 42% of the average.

summary: Cancer Research UK is the world's largest charitable funder of cancer research; this model covers all its charitable spending in the year to March 2026: research (£441m: grants, its own institutes and Cancer Research Horizons) and cancer information and influencing (£33m: policy campaigns and public information). Research is valued as a share of the world's cancer burden that a year of the field's research averts sooner, credited by Cancer Research UK's share of the world's cancer research funding, industry's included (about 0.6%); policy as its share of the health gain of the UK's smokefree-generation law (Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026); information as its share of the UK burden a year of everyone's cancer awareness work averts through earlier diagnosis; the deaths inside every branch's DALYs are valued by age, so mostly old deaths count less than DALYs' years lost. The result, about 0.00074 years of healthy life per $1,000, is low because research results arrive after about 15 years, are shared with a field that spends some $100bn a year, cancer mortality has fallen only slowly, and the result is counted as a past average at the next dollar's share; per dollar the policy work does about twenty times as well as the research, but it is 3% of the spending. All three branches are discounted for missing data, since none has measured outcomes for Cancer Research UK's own spending; the result is dominated by judgment (how much of the burden a year of research averts, how many years sooner, Cancer Research UK's share of the field) and is mostly uncertainty.

summary: Feeding America sources donated food from about 600 national food companies for the US network of more than 250 food banks and 60,000 pantries, funds and supports those food banks, and helps people apply for SNAP. It is low because the people helped are in the US, where $90 of food a year is a small share of what even a poor household spends, and because most of the resources behind the food are others'. About three fifths is the food, the rest SNAP help; both branches are discounted for missing data. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the food would have reached people without Feeding America, how poor the people served are, and how many SNAP enrolments the help causes.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Feeding America, food network programmes (FY2025)

name: First Embrace (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: small and premature newborns in public hospitals in Kano State, Nigeria.
summary: First Embrace runs kangaroo care, continuous skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding support, for small and premature newborns on public hospital wards in Kano State, Nigeria, paying and training the nurses. In its first year, 2026, at two hospitals, it costs about $180 per newborn enrolled; at the pilot hospital's own baseline about 1.9 × 10⁻¹ of these newborns died in their first month, and the 2026 Cochrane review finds kangaroo care cuts deaths by about 19%, counted only for the 80% of newborns who get at least 2 hours a day. It comes to about 5.2 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 1.0 – 11). The biggest uncertainties are the size of the effect at First Embrace's low daily dose and the baseline from 71 newborns; a randomised rollout across hospitals, which First Embrace plans, would settle both.

summary: GiveWell researches global health and poverty programmes and directs donors' money to the most cost-effective ones; this model covers a gift for its own operations in 2024 ($20.7M, audited), not the $163M of grants it paid out, which are the funded charities' cost and counted in their own models. Its operations aren't short of money (unrestricted gifts were five times its operating costs, the excess granted out), so a further dollar for them mostly frees another donor's dollar for grants and is worth about a dollar granted; the small rest does operations work, where each dollar moved about eleven dollars it caused in 2024 (a quarter of Open Philanthropy's money, all of it shifted, and 59% of other donors' giving, by its own donor survey with non-respondents counted at half, the $32M that fundraising organisations brought at GiveWell's share of the credit, plus $45M its research influenced), each dollar valued at the charities it went to, read live. At the defaults that comes to about 28 years of healthy life per $1,000, because a dollar for GiveWell ends up with GiveWell's grantees; the result moves most with the share freed for grants, the value of a life and the discount rate, and no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all of the result is the fortification branch, which GAIN reports only as a world total (1.55 billion people); split over its fortification countries with weight on the most populous (India, Nigeria, Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Ethiopia), a judgment, as GAIN publishes no country split.
summary: GAIN, a Geneva foundation, spent 61.6 million dollars on programmes in its year to June 2025: helping governments and food companies fortify salt, flour, oil and rice (1.55 billion people reached, by its own count), building markets and small businesses for nutritious food in Africa and Asia, workplace nutrition, and food-systems planning and policy. We estimate about 0.49 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, almost all from fortification: children's later earnings from iodized salt and less anaemia from iron-fortified food. The biggest uncertainty is how much of the yearly benefit of long-running national fortification programmes depends on GAIN's support (we count a quarter of the benefit as depending on outside support, and credit GAIN with about 25% of that support), and everything but the anaemia effect, which comes from evaluations of real fortification programmes, is discounted for missing data. The dollar is a past average (a year's spending over what it reached, not a price per item), so the result is scaled by our figure for GAIN's next dollar. With every judgment this uncertain, the result is mostly uncertainty: from 0.14 to 1.9 years per 1,000 dollars.

missing_data.note: Thin: GiveWell's 2014 salt iodization estimate: the cost per person is a generic figure for iodization plants, not GAIN's count of who got iodized salt, and GAIN's part in raising iodization is GiveWell's guessed 50% chance.

summary: GAIN helps governments and salt producers iodize salt so that children grow up without the iodine deficiency that lowers IQ. GiveWell's salt iodization analysis (built in 2014 for GAIN and the Iodine Global Network, moral weights updated in 2021) values the higher earnings of children who grow up with iodized salt, at about 7 times cash transfers. GiveWell's 50% chance that GAIN's work makes a difference and the size of the IQ gain drive the result.

rows.label: Cost of salt iodization per person per year

source.title: GiveWell, salt iodization cost-effectiveness analysis (2014, moral weights updated February 2021)

rows.explainer: GiveWell's best guess is the cost of iodizing salt in small plants, $0.10 per person per year (Horton, Mannar and Wesley 2008, Table 1); its other cases are large producers at $0.05 and the average, $0.08 (Parameters C47:D47), taken as the range. It is the cost of iodization itself, not GAIN's spending, and is per head of the whole population (see household coverage).

source.title: GiveWell, salt iodization cost-effectiveness analysis (2014, moral weights updated February 2021)

rows.explainer: GiveWell's judgment: higher than for deworming because there have been six randomised trials of iodine and cognition, but below 1 for their limitations. Range from GiveWell's pessimistic and optimistic cases (Parameters C48:D48).

rows.label: External validity

source.title: GiveWell, salt iodization cost-effectiveness analysis (2014, moral weights updated February 2021)

rows.explainer: GiveWell's judgment: the trials took place where deficiency was moderate, while some countries GAIN and the Iodine Global Network (then ICCIDD) work in are only mildly deficient; it also allows for national programmes being done less well than trials, and for the work preventing a slide back. GiveWell gives one figure; the range is ours.

source.title: GiveWell, salt iodization cost-effectiveness analysis (2014, moral weights updated February 2021)

rows.explainer: GiveWell assumes no leverage: GAIN and ICCIDD don't get governments to spend more on iodine than they would have, and GAIN's own case studies come to about $0.08 per extra person iodized, close to the cost of iodization itself. The optimistic case, 2, is the range.
