name: Habitat for Humanity International: public awareness, education and housing advocacy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Home Equals carries the result (the US branch is a small net harm, so 0); shares follow each country's contribution, each region a quarter of the people (a judgment).
summary: Habitat for Humanity International's (HFHI) public awareness and education programme ($24.3 million in the year to June 2025, plus an estimated $3.5 million of advocacy booked in its other programmes) runs Habitat's media, website and learning events and its housing-policy advocacy: in the US, where the Habitat network counts $6.65 billion of state and local housing money in FY2025 ($369 million in FY2026), and worldwide through the Home Equals campaign for informal settlements ($3.7 billion of government money and 23.7 million people since 2023, Habitat's counts). We value the money as housing for the households it reaches, with spillovers and child deaths averted, net of what it costs the taxpayers who pay for it, on the site's log-income scale, with the research on whether advocacy changes policy and HFHI's small share of the coalitions behind the wins. Households and payers are on the same household-survey scale, so the gain and the cost nearly cancel: the US branch is a small net harm, the Home Equals branch a small net good, and the result is a small net good. Both branches are discounted for missing data. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the money reaches households, how much poorer they are than those who pay, and how much of it the advocacy caused.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Habitat for Humanity International, public awareness and education (FY2025)

name: Habitat for Humanity International: international programme (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Habitat's work in more than 60 countries, by region at the shares of the result at the defaults (Africa 50%, Asia and the Pacific 22%, Europe and the Middle East 16%, Latin America and the Caribbean 13%), each region's share spread equally over the stand-in countries whose survey consumption the build reads (a judgment).
summary: Habitat for Humanity International (HFHI) spent $75.5 million in the year to June 2025 helping families outside the US build, extend and repair homes with Habitat national organisations in more than 60 countries (about 470,000 people across the network, mostly incremental building and repairs), and working with lenders and building-material firms so that low-income households can buy housing loans and products (2.4 million people in Habitat's count). We value the net housing subsidy families receive on the site's log-income scale, at the household-survey consumption of Habitat's families in each region, plus a small surplus for the partners' customers, and credit HFHI with its share of all the resources behind the network's housing (about a fifth: the national organisations raise most of the money). Close to 60% of the families are in middle-income Latin America, Europe and the Middle East, housing is an in-kind transfer, and both branches are discounted for missing data: HFHI publishes no subsidy per family and no split of its spending by type of work. Those are the biggest uncertainties, with the families' consumption. The market branch is a past average, so it reads Habitat's next-dollar figure.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Habitat for Humanity International, international programme (FY2025)

name: Habitat for Humanity International: US affiliates (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: HFHI's US affiliates.
summary: Habitat for Humanity International (HFHI) funds and supports about 984 independent US affiliates that build homes with volunteers and sell them at appraised value to low-income families on zero-interest mortgages, and that repair low-income owners' homes: about 3,400 homes and 12,370 repairs in the year to June 2025, plus disaster recovery. We count the net subsidy each family receives (the home's value less the market value of what it repays and its sweat equity) on the site's log-income scale, and credit HFHI with its share of all the resources behind the homes: the affiliates raise most of the money and spend about twice the sale price per home. Two things set the result: the families are in the US, where a dollar of housing adds little to consumption, and a dollar of the network's resources delivers under half a dollar of subsidy. The biggest uncertainties are the affiliates' full cost per home and how much a housing subsidy is worth to a family against cash. All three branches are discounted for missing data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Habitat for Humanity International, US affiliates programme (FY2025)

summary: Helen Keller Intl supports governments' twice-yearly campaigns that give children aged 6 to 59 months vitamin A capsules. The Life You Can Save estimates a cost per DALY averted in each of 13 African countries from Helen Keller Intl's 2024 costs and children reached, a 12% fall in child deaths for the six months a dose protects, and each country's child death rate. Our view values the deaths averted the site's way and takes out the doses governments would have given anyway; the biggest uncertainties are how much vitamin A still cuts deaths where deficiency has fallen and how much of the coverage is Helen Keller Intl's doing.

rows.label: Ratio of value generated from income increases to value generated from mortalities averted among people under age 15 by VAS (overall), at your discount rate and values
rows.explainer: Changed for consistency. GiveWell values long-term income here as a fixed share of the value of the deaths averted, a ratio it took from its AMF and SMC models at its own values: income discounted at 4% over 40 years starting 10 years on, 1/ln 2 units of value per unit of ln(consumption), and its weight on a death. So in the sheet the income gain would grow with the weight on a life and ignore the discount rate, unlike in AMF and SMC. Our view rescales the ratio: the present value of those 40 years at your discount rate over the same at 4%, times the income slider over 1/ln 2, divided by the weight on a life (which the value of deaths it multiplies already carries). At the defaults it is the sheet's ratio; the evaluator view keeps it.

name: HIAS: US advocacy and litigation for refugees
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees waiting abroad for US resettlement, by the largest nationalities in the pipeline (the DRC, Afghanistan, Venezuela, Syria, Myanmar, Sudan, Somalia, Guatemala); a judgment.
summary: HIAS spends about $3 million a year (our estimate, inside its US accounts line) on US advocacy, community engagement and litigation, chiefly as a plaintiff in Pacito v. Trump against the January 2025 suspension of refugee admissions, which let more than 80 approved refugees travel in 2025 before the Ninth Circuit reversed most of the injunction in March 2026. We value the pending case as a small chance (2%) of restoring about 10,000 admissions a year for the years a win counts, fiscal 2025 carrying half of the case's cost, and the 2025 admissions as won, each refugee gaining the US level of consumption over decades against the level where they wait, with HIAS credited 15% of the litigation; at HIAS's own next-dollar figure (49%) it comes to about 0.0039 years of healthy life per $1,000, because a refugee resettled in the US gains several doublings of consumption for decades. The result is mostly uncertainty (the chance of success, HIAS's share and the years a win counts span over a thousandfold), and it is discounted for missing data.

name: HIAS: programmes for refugees abroad
beneficiaries_note: Our build: HIAS's country programmes weighted by our judgment of where the spending and the result go, as HIAS publishes no spending by country: Chad (257,700 served, many through cheap camp-wide services, and most of the cash), then Colombia, Ecuador and Panama (36,700, about 21,000 and 23,000 served, with more cash per person and the legal work), Ukraine and Moldova (32,300), Costa Rica, Mexico, Venezuela, Kenya, Israel, Greece and the Resettlement Support Center in Austria (Form 990 Schedule O).
summary: HIAS spent $48.1 million in the year to September 2025 on programmes for refugees and displaced people in about 15 countries, the largest for Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad and for Venezuelans and others across Latin America: cash and basic needs for 54,000 people (33,000 in Chad), legal protection for 81,000, violence prevention and support for 80,500, mental-health support for 73,100, child protection for 127,000 children and economic inclusion for 6,000 (calendar 2025 counts), and the US Resettlement Support Center in Austria until admissions stopped. Each activity is built from the research on that kind of work: cash and goods on the site's log-income scale (with a few crisis deaths averted in Chad's camps), legal status from Colombia's regularisation natural experiment, mental-health, survivors' and children's support in life satisfaction from humanitarian trials, economic inclusion from the graduation trials, and the refugees processed for the US by the consumption they gain there. It comes to about 0.044 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.025 – 0.078), because much of the spending is on protection and legal work whose measurable gains are small per person; cash in Chad gives over half of it. Every branch is discounted for missing data: HIAS counts the people reached but publishes no controlled measure of its own results; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, displaced people's consumption and the share of the payments that reaches people as cash.

name: HIAS: refugee resettlement and legal services in the US
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees, asylum seekers and other immigrants served in the US (resettlement and legal services).
summary: HIAS spent $58.7 million of its own money in the US in the year to September 2025 on refugee resettlement through about 30 local partner agencies, integration and social services, and immigration legal services for 1,433 clients, helped by $18.7 million of pro bono lawyers' time that we count as their contribution, not HIAS's cost. Resettlement is valued as the money and goods clients receive and a short head start in work, on the site's log-income scale at newly arrived refugees' consumption; legal help as the extra chance a represented asylum seeker wins the right to stay, their consumption and their remittances home against their country of origin's over the years they stay, and the deaths a removal risks. name: Innocence Project (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: wrongly convicted people in US prisons and their families (exonerations, reforms that prevent wrongful convictions, compensation).
summary: The Innocence Project is a US legal organisation (31.5 million dollars spent in the year to June 2025) that frees wrongly convicted people, mostly with DNA evidence, campaigns for laws that prevent wrongful convictions and compensate exonerees, and supports the Innocence Network's groups. Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over what those years achieved: about a third of the credit for its 24 exonerations (the years in prison they would still have served, the deaths prison causes, and compensation counted as a transfer, the exoneree's gain less the taxpayers' cost), shared with pro bono law firms that give about as much as it spends, about a third of a small cut in wrongful imprisonment from the eyewitness, interrogation, discovery and compensation laws it won or defended, and a small share of other innocence groups' exonerations; every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.00019 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: its casework costs about two million dollars per exoneration, each freeing one person from about a dozen more years in prison; the reforms of the window remove only about 1% of the country's wrongful imprisonment; and the next dollar counts at a third of the average as it holds over three years of spending in reserve. The model's own ranges span more than a thousandfold, so the result is mostly uncertainty; the biggest are how many people in US prisons are innocent, how much the window's reforms cut that, and the Innocence Project's share of the coalitions behind the reforms.

name: Iodine Global Network: salt iodization support (charityevals, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by branch, each split by births: policy reviews and tools 21% (India 83% of its births, then Tanzania, Cameroon, Germany, South Sudan, Sri Lanka and smaller countries), Lebanon 31%, Vietnam 26%, producer quality assurance 15% (Bolivia, Madagascar, Mozambique, northern Argentina and Peru by the births reached), regional advocacy 6% (South Asia's four uncounted countries, five large European countries and North America by births; a judgment), Davao City under 1%.
summary: The Iodine Global Network (IGN) helps governments and salt producers keep salt iodized: in 2025, spending $1.32 million, it brought Lebanon's main producers back to national standards, improved small producers' salt in Bolivia, northern Argentina and Madagascar, gave evidence behind Vietnam's Ministry of Health recommending that iodized salt stay compulsory in processed foods (the final decree is still being drafted), helped Davao City restart salt enforcement, reviewed laws or applied its monitoring tools in 19 countries, and pressed for iodine policy in Europe, South Asia and North America. Each piece of work is valued by the births it moves from iodine deficiency to protection (the reviews and advocacy in new rules the size of Moldova's requirement of iodized salt in bread, one every two and every four years): 7.5 IQ points lost to deficiency, halved for the milder deficiency at stake, worth 0.67% higher earnings per point over 40 working years, plus goitre averted less hyperthyroidism caused, counted for the years a won change counts (producer support for two or three) and credited by IGN's share of the resources behind it. The result, about 0.83 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, is very uncertain and rests mostly on judgment (how many new rules the reviews and advocacy lead to, how much mild deficiency harms cognition, whether Vietnam's final decree keeps the requirement); every branch is discounted for missing data, since no change in iodine status is measured, and the next dollar counts at 56% of the past average.

name: Kaya Guides (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: young adults across India, mostly in Hindi-speaking states, reached on WhatsApp.
summary: Kaya Guides runs WHO's guided self-help course for depression, Step-by-Step, on WhatsApp in Hindi for young adults in India: eight weeks of video lessons with short weekly calls from lay guides. In 2025 about 2,800 people started it, at about $60 each. The effect is the three randomised trials of guided Step-by-Step pooled (about half a standard deviation on depression), fading over about a year and a half, cut for trust in the trials and how far they carry to young Indians on WhatsApp and for engagement, plus the suicides it averts. It comes to about 0.78 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.23 – 2.1). The biggest uncertainties are how long the effect lasts and how much of the trials' effect carries over; Kaya Guides' own randomised trial, running in 2026, will test both.

summary: Kids in Need of Defense (KIND) represents unaccompanied migrant children in US immigration proceedings through its own lawyers and about 4,600 pro bono attorneys, and supports children in Mexico, Central America and Europe; in 2024 it served 8,500 children in the US and closed 580 cases with permanent relief (asylum, green cards, T and U visas). The biggest uncertainties are the chance of removal without status and what a lawyer changes, both judged from observational data, so all four branches (US casework, Central American Minors refugee applications, psychosocial support in Mexico and for Ukrainian children, and the other children served outside the US) are discounted by the shared missing-data slider; KIND's advocacy is a separate model.

name: LABRI (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the one policy whose expected value is counted is the Philippines', so the children and adults protected are in the Philippines.
summary: LABRI (the Lead-Acid Battery Recycling Initiative) works with governments to stop used car and motorbike batteries being melted down in backyards, which spreads lead into the air and soil; in the Philippines it has proposed, with the environmental regulator, making battery makers and importers responsible for licensed recycling, and is now designing that policy with government and industry. We count its spending from April 2025 to October 2026 against that work's expected value: the chance the policy is adopted, times the blood lead Philippine children would lose, valued as later earnings, with adults' heart-disease deaths as a side effect. At the defaults it comes to about 0.0 years of healthy life per $1,000. Nothing has been adopted yet, the charity publishes no accounts and nobody has measured how much of children's blood lead comes from battery recycling, so the result is mostly uncertainty and is discounted for missing data.

name: Lead Exposure Elimination Project (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by country, each country's births times its branch's discounted years and its own delivery share (regulations 35%, Nigeria at half credit; market switches 65%, Pakistan at its measured 53%, Malawi 90%, the other five 20%).
summary: The Lead Exposure Elimination Project (LEEP) tests paint on sale in low- and middle-income countries and works with governments and manufacturers to take lead out of it; we count its spending from its founding in September 2020 to the end of 2025 against what it won: lead paint rules adopted in seven countries with its support (Nigeria at half credit) and measured switches to lead-free paint in seven more, Pakistan the largest. Each year a market stays free of lead paint spares about a birth cohort the IQ points that paint lead would cost them, valued as later earnings; adults' lead deaths in the same homes are a side effect. At the defaults it comes to about 5.4 years of healthy life per $1,000, but the result is mostly uncertainty: no study measures how much of children's blood lead comes from paint in these countries, and the discount rate and the years a won rule counts move it most, since the benefits come decades later. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and its spices, eyeliner and plastics work has won no change yet, so it counts as cost only.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Lead Exposure Elimination Project

summary: The Lead Exposure Elimination Project tests paint on sale in low- and middle-income countries and helps governments bring in and enforce lead paint limits and manufacturers switch. name: League of Women Voters Education Fund (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends and reforms (the redistricting branch's people are in the US states that adopted commissions); the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: The League of Women Voters Education Fund, the 501(c)(3) of the League of Women Voters (the League of Women Voters of the United States is a 501(c)(4), and gifts to it aren't tax-deductible, so this models the Education Fund only), spent $11.3 million of its own money in the year to June 2025, beside $5.4 million of donated legal services and advertising that count as the donors' resources, on VOTE411.org, voter registration, voting-rights litigation and reform campaigns. Four branches: its direct work's share of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (about 36% of the result); its voter information and registration, 73% of its spending, credited in the same cut at the shared weight for turnout and civic-education dollars (about 36%); its 1% share of the movement that moved 79 million Americans' maps to redistricting commissions since 2008 (about 13%); and its other reforms (voting access, the Electoral College, DC statehood), judged a quarter as effective per dollar as the redistricting movement (about 16%). With its next dollar at 52.5% of the average, it comes to about 0.0034 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars; the result turns most on the years a win counts, the field's effect on the risk (both judgments), the income gain of democracy and the next-dollar figure, and all four branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: the one programme, in Iganga District, Eastern Uganda (2025 Pilot Report p. 2).
summary: Learning Alliance gives primary-school teachers in Iganga District, Eastern Uganda, daily scripted phonics lessons, training and coaching visits every few weeks; in 2025, its first year, it spent about $240,000 on 20,000 pupils in Primary 1 to 3 in 75 schools. name: Macmillan Cancer Support: information, support and care for people with cancer in the UK (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Macmillan works only in the UK.
summary: Macmillan Cancer Support helps people with cancer in the UK: a phone line with cancer nurses, information advisers and welfare rights advisers, an online community, information centres, volunteer Buddies and small grants, plus learning for the 11,100 NHS nurses and other professionals in its network, funding for community and end-of-life care, and grants to community groups. Our model of all its charitable spending in 2025 (£112m in the year; 476,000 people with cancer supported) values the support by its effect on wellbeing, from trials of telephone and online support for people with cancer, and the welfare benefits its advisers help people claim on the site's log-income scale, net of what they cost taxpayers. It comes to about 0.0017 years of healthy life per $1,000, because the help is light (a call or two, or reading a forum) for people who already have NHS care, and its biggest money gain, benefits identified at about £8,500 a year for each of 13,200 households (about £5,100 awarded), is mostly a transfer from other UK households that are only somewhat richer. About half of the result comes from those benefits. Every branch but the grants (audited money paid) is discounted for missing data, since none of Macmillan's services has a controlled evaluation: the Support Line, Buddies and online support, welfare rights, the professionals and the posts its grants paid for, and the community and system work. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the identified benefits are paid and would not have been claimed anyway, and how far below average the claimants' consumption is; with every judgment at its ends the result spans over a thousandfold, so it is mostly uncertainty.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: wishes granted by Make-A-Wish America's national office and 58 chapters to children in the US and its territories.
summary: Make-A-Wish America and its 58 chapters grant wishes (trips, meetings, gifts) to children aged 2½ to 17 with critical illnesses: 16,295 in fiscal 2024 (September 2023 to August 2024), at about $21,600 a wish with fundraising and management. name: Malaria Consortium, malaria emergency response in South Ethiopia (The Life You Can Save, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: The model's name: Malaria Consortium, malaria emergency response in South Ethiopia (The Life You Can Save, 2025).

missing_data.note: Thin: the effect is the before-and-after change in the project districts' monitoring indicators (malaria cases relative to the region's, admissions, case fatality), with no comparison group, read as a fall in incidence across the whole population.

summary: Malaria Consortium ran an emergency malaria response with the health authorities in 18 high-burden districts of South Ethiopia from mid-2024, after cases in Ethiopia rose eightfold. The Life You Can Save reads the fall in the districts' malaria indicators over the project as cases, admissions and deaths averted and estimates $225 per DALY averted. Our view values each death averted by age the site's way and credits Malaria Consortium with most but not all of the change; the biggest uncertainty is how much of the fall the project caused.

name: Malaria Consortium, digital net campaigns in South Sudan (The Life You Can Save, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: The model's name: Malaria Consortium, digital net campaigns in South Sudan (The Life You Can Save, 2025).

missing_data.note: Measured: the campaign's own household registration counted the people reached and the 13.55% more people found than projected, and the effect of nets on malaria and children's deaths is from the Cochrane review of randomised trials.

summary: Malaria Consortium supported South Sudan's health ministry in moving its mass bednet campaigns from paper to phones, registering and geo-tagging households. The Life You Can Save credits it with the 13.55% more people the digital registration found than the projections, counts the cost of their nets as well as Malaria Consortium's own, and estimates $98 per DALY averted. Our view takes the nets out of the cost and nets their money from the good instead, values each child's death averted by age the site's way and discounts the net's later years; the biggest uncertainty is whether the extra people found would otherwise have gone without nets.

name: Malaria Consortium, vitamin A with seasonal malaria chemoprevention in Bauchi, Nigeria (The Life You Can Save, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: The model's name: Malaria Consortium, vitamin A with seasonal malaria chemoprevention in Bauchi, Nigeria (The Life You Can Save, 2025).

missing_data.note: Measured: Malaria Consortium's baseline and endline coverage surveys of the integrated SMC and vitamin A cycle, and effects from trials of SMC (Mali) and the Cochrane review of vitamin A supplementation.

summary: Malaria Consortium added vitamin A capsules to the door-to-door seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) campaign in two areas of Bauchi state, Nigeria, in 2021, raising vitamin A coverage from 1% to 83%. The Life You Can Save credits the programme with the deaths averted by the vitamin A and SMC coverage added, at $1.18 a child, and estimates $11 per DALY averted. Our view values each child's death averted by age the site's way and counts only what the one round costed buys: a quarter of a season's SMC effect and half a year's vitamin A effect. The biggest uncertainties are the baseline SMC coverage the sheet assumes and how much protection one round gives.

name: Mercy Corps (Prosper Global): all programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Mercy Corps' programme spending and grants by region from its US entity's Form 990 Schedule F, fiscal 2025 (Sub-Saharan Africa 52%, the Middle East and North Africa 15%, Russia and neighbouring states 11%, South America 9%, South Asia 5%, East Asia and the Pacific 4%, Central America and the Caribbean 3%), each region split equally over Mercy Corps' main programme countries there (a judgment: no country split is published).
summary: Mercy Corps (renamed Prosper Global in 2026) spent $509 million on programmes in its year to June 2025, half of it in Sub-Saharan Africa: livelihoods and market systems ($207M), emergency relief ($138M, mostly cash, water and supplies through partners in Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine and elsewhere), peace, governance and education ($90M), health and nutrition ($43M) and recovery ($31M). It counts people reached (over 36 million) but publishes no controlled measure of what its spending achieved, so every branch is built from its spending, its reach or a judged cost per person and the research on that kind of work, and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.17 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.083 – 0.52: the result is mostly uncertainty): half from livelihoods (small consumption gains spread over the 19 million people its economic programmes reach), a third from relief (cash and goods, and a few excess crisis deaths averted), little from water, nutrition, education and peace work. The biggest uncertainties are how much the livelihood programmes raise consumption for the many people they reach only indirectly, the missing-data discount, and crisis-affected people's consumption.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Mercy Corps, all programmes

name: New Incentives (The Life You Can Save, 2025)
beneficiaries_note: The location the sheet's bottom line reads (row labels naming Nigeria).

missing_data.note: Partly thin (50%): New Incentives counts the infants it enrolled, but the deaths and illness are the Lives Saved Tool's estimate of Nigeria's national rise in coverage, credited by New Incentives' share of the country's under-fives rather than the vaccinations it was measured to add.

summary: New Incentives gives mothers in northern Nigeria small cash payments when they bring their infants for routine vaccinations. The Life You Can Save credits it with its share (by infants enrolled) of the child deaths and illness that Nigeria's rise in vaccine coverage from 2022 to 2024 averted, from the Lives Saved Tool and the literature, at New Incentives' $17 per infant. Our view values the deaths the site's way, counts illness for as long as it lasts and cuts tuberculosis to New Incentives' share; the biggest uncertainty is whether the national coverage gain is a fair measure of what New Incentives added.

name: No Means No Worldwide
beneficiaries_note: Our build: girls taught the No Means No course in 2025 across six countries; NMNW publishes no split, so a judgment from its 2025 report (Nigeria's and Zimbabwe's national scale-ups, South Africa's 90-minute course to tens of thousands, Uganda's partners) and 2024's (Mozambique, Eswatini).
summary: No Means No Worldwide writes a 10-hour school course that teaches girls to recognise, resist and escape sexual assault (and boys to respect consent and step in) and trains local partners and teachers to give it; in 2025 it spent $1.51 million and its partners taught 128,000 young people in six African countries, about half of them a new 90-minute version. Two cluster-randomised trials of the girls' course found almost half fewer rapes in the following year, but a third, with independent data collectors, found none two years on; each rape averted spares about 0.3 of a healthy year of post-traumatic stress and depression and a small risk of suicide, which after adjustments comes to about 0.10 years of healthy life per $1,000. The result is mostly uncertainty: whether the trials' effect is real, how long it lasts and how common rape is among the girls taught. The 90-minute course, never tested against a control group, counts at a fifth of the full course's effect and is discounted for missing data.

name: Norwegian Refugee Council: advocacy and information (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all of the result is humanitarian funding kept or added across the appeals, the rest access in Sudan and the DRC; spread like NRC's programmes by its 2025 project revenue by country office (Annual Accounts 2025, note 2), as a stand-in for the crises the appeals fund; a judgment.
summary: The Norwegian Refugee Council's advocacy and information work (NOK 256 million, $25 million, in 2025): campaigning against the 2025 humanitarian funding gap and for access in Sudan and the DRC, media work and the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre's data. It publishes no measured result, so both branches are built from ranged judgments and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: NRC's share of the aid that NGOs' funding advocacy kept or added, net of the aid it displaces (about 97% of the result), and the extra aid access gains let through, net of the same (about 3%), plus a judged share for its other work, each dollar of aid at the site's shared value of a humanitarian dollar. It comes to about 0.0049 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.00024 – 0.058), because a dollar of humanitarian aid is worth about a fifth of cash to the poor (the site's relief models with nothing taken off for missing data; this model's own missing-data step applies once) and NRC's share of the aid moved is small; the result is mostly uncertainty, judgments on how much aid advocacy moves and NRC's part in it driving it.

name: Norwegian Refugee Council: programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: NRC's 2025 project revenue by country office (Annual Accounts 2025, note 2: NOK 7,276m over 39 country offices, NORCAP, regional offices and Norway left out), as the spread of its programmes; the branches' results aren't split by country, so this weights every country by its spending (Ukraine 13%, Sudan 11%).
summary: The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) spent NOK 8.7 billion ($837 million) in 2025 helping people displaced by conflict and disaster in 39 countries, mostly with government and UN grants: cash and vouchers (two fifths in Ukraine, a quarter in Sudan), food security, shelter, education, water and sanitation, legal assistance and protection for 10.6 million people, plus 613 NORCAP expert secondments to UN agencies and governments. NRC counts the people each programme reached and the cash it hands out, but publishes no controlled evaluation of its own, so the cash transfers count in full and every other part, built from spending, reach and the research on its kind of work, is counted at half by the shared missing-data slider. It comes to about 0.20 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.11 – 0.38): cash carries about 35%, education's later earnings about 30%, food security about 15%, shelter, water and sanitation, legal assistance, NORCAP and protection the rest. NRC is phasing out food security by 2027, so a dollar given now buys a little more cash and less food security than in 2025; the biggest uncertainties are how much emergency education raises later earnings and how much of a crisis's excess deaths basic-needs aid averts.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Norwegian Refugee Council, programmes (2025)

name: Novah
beneficiaries_note: Our build: NOVAH's radio drama aired in Rwanda only in 2025.
summary: NOVAH makes Twubakane, a radio drama about a Rwandan couple that learns to decide together, to prevent violence against women by their partners. In 2025 it spent $173,600: its first six-episode season aired on a regional station in northern Rwanda and about 27,000 adults followed it, and the money also made a second season for a 2026 trial. With partner violence falling by a judged quarter among couples who listen (a trial of similar videos in Uganda, and NOVAH's own small pilot) and each year of violence costing about 4.6 × 10⁻² healthy years by the Global Burden of Disease's count, it comes to about 0.063 years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainties are whether the drama reduces violence at all and how much harm a year of violence averted spares; until NOVAH's own trial reports, the effect is discounted for missing data.

name: One for the World (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each recipient its donors give to, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: One for the World asks students and young professionals in the US, UK, Canada and Australia to give 1% of their income to charities GiveWell recommends, through chapters at universities and graduate schools and talks at companies; this model covers its year to June 2024 ($758K of its own costs across its US company and UK charity; donors' money passed on is left out). At the defaults it averts about 2.0 years of healthy life per $1,000: its 166 new pledges and the year's new corporate donors' discounted lifetime giving (at the yearly gift of its active pledgers, on the shared pledge curve lowered for its faster attrition) and the year's one-off gifts, of which it caused about half (its own strict count: 44%), come to $720,000, of which $420,000 is credited to it once the credit for the money to GiveWell's recommended charities (84%) is shared with GiveWell, whose research directed it, each dollar valued at its donors' charities, half counted as new money, the next dollar at 57% of the past average. The money it moves goes almost all to top global-health charities, and it causes about one dollar of discounted giving per dollar it spends. The result moves most with the discount rate, its next-dollar figure, its own count of what it caused and the value of a child's life; no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

name: Oxygen Access Project: oxygen care for hypoxaemic children in Gombe State, Nigeria (charityevals)
summary: Oxygen Access Project helps 23 state secondary hospitals in Gombe State, Nigeria, find children whose blood oxygen is low (below 90%) and treat them with oxygen, with the state hospitals board and the Nigerian NGO Taimaka. This model counts the children's deaths averted in its first financial year (14 February to 31 December 2025, about 660 hypoxaemic children recorded from April) against that year's spending, and comes to 3.5 years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainty is how many deaths better oxygen care averts here: before-after studies of oxygen systems found pneumonia deaths falling by about half, but the one randomised trial in Nigeria found no further fall once pulse oximetry was in place, and the charity has not yet measured who got oxygen or who died. So the effect is discounted for weak evidence and the model for missing data.

name: Prison Policy Initiative (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: incarcerated people and their families in the United States (federal phone caps, state free-call laws, decarceration).
summary: Prison Policy Initiative is a small US research and advocacy group on mass incarceration (1.9 million dollars spent in the year to June 2025). Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over the wins of those years: a share of the federal caps on prison and jail phone rates that the Martha Wright-Reed Act of 2022 made possible (still saving families about 250 million dollars a year after the FCC raised the caps in 2025), a smaller share of five states' free-call laws and other fee and visiting wins, a very small share of the people kept out of prison by the reforms its data fed (their better years and the deaths a year in prison causes), and half the credit for ending prison gerrymandering in several states, each valued on the site's shared scales; every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.016 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: about two thirds of it is deaths averted by decarceration, while money saved by poor American families is worth little on a scale set by the world's poorest, and PPI holds about five years of spending in reserve, so the next dollar counts at a quarter of the average. The biggest uncertainties are PPI's share of the decarceration and phone-rate campaigns and how long the caps hold.

name: Protect Democracy: defending US democracy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends; the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: Protect Democracy litigates, builds tools and coalitions and writes policy to keep the United States from sliding into a more authoritarian government ($34.4 million in 2024). Its year of work is counted as its share of the money behind the US pro-democracy field's work against backsliding (about 1.3%) times the share of the forecast chance of the US leaving the democracies before 2030 (about 11%) that a year of the field's work removes (judged 4.5%); the loss is the income democracy brings (Acemoglu et al. 2019), building over 25 years, put off by the years a win counts and lasting until the slide would be undone (5% a year), and democracy's other goods. A smaller branch counts its work for proportional representation (about a twelfth of the result). With its next dollar at 35% of the average that comes to about 0.0054 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges spanning over ten thousandfold; the biggest is the field's effect on that chance, a judgment with no study behind it. Both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

name: Refugee Council: advocacy and awareness raising (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: UK asylum and refugee policy, for people in the UK asylum system.
summary: The Refugee Council's advocacy and awareness raising (research, policy, parliamentary work, campaigns, media and its new brand: £4.3m over the two years to March 2025) is counted as a past average against what those years won: the government's pilot doubling the move-on period for newly recognised refugees from 28 to 56 days (from December 2024; ended for single adults in September 2025), and the restart of asylum processing with the Rwanda plan scrapped. Valued as extra days of housing and support for about 31,600 refugees a year over the pilot and as claims decided instead of left in limbo for about 29,000 arrivals a year, with 30% of the move-on change and 5% of the other caused by campaigning, the Refugee Council's share of the campaigners 25% and 12%, and its next dollar at 42% of the average, a dollar does about 0.00088 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.00021 – 0.0034). That is low because the people helped are in the UK and most of the change came from the new government's own plans. The result is mostly judgment (how much of each win campaigning caused spans ten-fold) and is discounted for missing data; any lasting change to the move-on period after March 2025 is left for the next year's accounts.

name: Refugee Council: therapeutic services (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees and people seeking asylum in England, helped where they live now.
summary: The Refugee Council's Therapeutic Services (£1.74m in the year to March 2025) gave one-to-one, group, child and family therapy to 303 refugees and people seeking asylum who had been through trauma, plus an uncounted number of children in its MyView service (judged about 50). The effect is the Cochrane-method review of psychosocial interventions for refugees (Turrini et al. 2019: about 1 SD on depression against waitlist or usual care), fading over about a year and a half, cut to about 0.3 of that by trust in small heterogeneous trials, what clients would have got anyway, the Refugee Council's share of the credit and incomplete courses, plus the suicides it averts. It comes to about 0.0026 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.00087 – 0.0074), low because each person costs about $7,000 and a WELLBY is worth a fifteenth of a healthy year at the site's rate. The branch is discounted for missing data (no evaluation of the Refugee Council's own therapy, which mixes psychotherapy, art and music therapy and groups rather than the trials' protocols); the biggest uncertainties are how much of the trials' effect carries over and how long it lasts.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Refugee Council (UK), therapeutic services (year to March 2025)

name: Refugee Council: resettlement, children's services, integration and destitution (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees and people seeking asylum in England, helped where they live now.
summary: The Refugee Council is the UK's national refugee charity; this model covers its four service lines in the year to March 2025 (£12.25m): casework for about 1,700 refugees resettled with English councils, advice, housing and asylum-support help for about 6,500 people seeking asylum and newly recognised refugees, and advice, reception and youth work for 7,022 separated children and young people. It comes to about 0.0018 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.00077 – 0.0045): the help is valued at its money and wellbeing worth to clients in the UK, who consume many times what the people overseas aid reaches do, and councils and the Home Office would commission much of it from someone else. About half the result is resettlement (benefits and earnings brought forward), two-fifths integration and destitution (support secured, homelessness averted) and the rest children's services, including children moved from adult hotels into care after age-dispute challenges. The biggest uncertainties are what the help is worth to each client and how much others would have given anyway; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no outcome is measured against a comparison group.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. Haitians paroled into the US (about 42%, counted as Haiti's), Sudan's humanitarian response and access from Chad (about 23%), asylum seekers' work permits in Costa Rica (about 5%); the other campaigns (about 30%) over Ukraine, Gaza, the US and Uganda by the annual report's emphasis (a judgment).
summary: Refugees International, a Washington advocacy group that takes no government money, spent $4.5m on advocacy and strategic outreach in 2024 (its latest full audited year). No outcome is measured, so each of its main 2024 results is built from public data and ranged judgments and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: the roughly 97,000 Haitians paroled into the US that year under pathways it pressed for, valued by their gain in consumption and health, and their remittances home, for the years they stay; Sudan's $1.9bn 2024 humanitarian response, of which advocacy is credited with a small share, net of the aid it displaced, and the aid the reopened Adre crossing let through; and Costa Rica's June 2024 reform giving asylum seekers work permits, from a study of regularisation in Colombia; other campaigns add 42%. It comes to about 0.040 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.0075 – 0.26): about two fifths from Haiti, a quarter from Sudan, a twentieth from Costa Rica and the rest from the other campaigns. summary: The RepresentUs Education Fund, the 501(c)(3) of the US anti-corruption and democracy-reform group RepresentUs (Represent.Us itself is a 501(c)(4), and gifts to it aren't tax-deductible, so this models the Education Fund only), spent $7.8 million in 2024 on national videos and social media about corruption and threats to democracy, education and volunteer outreach behind state and local ballot measures, research, the American Democracy Summit and grants to Represent.Us for campaign outreach. With its next dollar at 49% of the average, it comes to about 0.0077 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars; the result is mostly judgment (the years a win counts, how much a voting reform changes how well people are governed, the split of its spending between the branches), and all four branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

name: Respira Health: WhatsApp pulmonary rehabilitation in India (charityevals)
summary: Respira Health runs an eight-week pulmonary rehabilitation programme by WhatsApp chatbot, with physiotherapists on video calls, for adults in India who are breathless from COPD or other chronic lung disease. This model counts its first year (April 2025 to March 2026: scoping in India, a breathlessness education test and a pilot that enrolled 51 people) against that year's spending, and comes to 0.0038 years of healthy life per $1,000. Most of the year went on setting the programme up, so the cost per participant is high; the charity hopes to enrol about 1,000 people in its second year. Participants did about a third of the exercise sessions on average, and the pilot had no control group, so the gain in health is taken from studies of supervised rehabilitation and discounted for missing data. Its spending isn't published: the year's cost is our estimate from the money it raised and its budget.

name: The Salvation Army USA: overseas work (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. The operating support (schools, health care, social services and church life in the territories that can't pay their own way, 48%) follows International Headquarters' maintenance grants by territory (International Trust accounts 2025, Note 11), split equally over each territory's countries; SAWSO's livelihoods and anti-trafficking work (50%) is spread equally over the low- and middle-income countries its report lists; relief goes to Ukraine and the countries hosting its refugees, education projects to Rwanda and the Republic of the Congo (judgments where no split is published).
summary: The Salvation Army USA's overseas work, about 2.4% of its programme spending ($69.7 million in fiscal 2025): the World Service Office's (SAWSO) grants to Salvation Army units abroad for disaster relief (mostly Ukrainian refugees), livelihoods (savings groups and income generation), education, health and anti-trafficking, and its and the US territories' support for the territories that can't pay their own way (maintenance grants, an endowment for officers' support and the running of International Headquarters), five-sixths of the money, which pays for their schools, health care, social services and church life. SAWSO publishes no count of people reached or of outcomes, so every branch is built from the research on its kind of work with its own spending (a meta-analysis of savings-promotion trials, the returns to schooling, the Cochrane review of community newborn care, studies of what relief costs to deliver, churchgoing and life satisfaction), and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.25 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.088 – 0.73), about 50 times the US work per dollar, because a dollar does far more on the log scale for a poor household; the money is spread over church running costs and small projects with no measured effect, and the result is mostly uncertainty. The biggest uncertainties are how much savings groups raise consumption and what they cost per household (the meta-analysis finds a small gain, the largest trial none), what a school place costs and how many pupils would otherwise not be in school, and how much of the support pays for services rather than worship.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: The Salvation Army USA, overseas work

name: The Salvation Army USA: services in the US (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the Salvation Army's services in the US (its overseas work has its own model).
summary: The Salvation Army is a church that runs the largest network of social services in the United States: food (184 million meals), shelters (10 million nights), help with bills, holiday gifts, housing placements, residential addiction recovery funded by its thrift stores, and community centres. Our model of every US programme in fiscal 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), with the thrift stores' running costs, clients' day-care fees and the overseas work (a model of its own) left out, values the food, goods, bills and services at what families would otherwise pay on the site's log-income scale, shelter by a room's value and the deaths it averts, housing placements by the trials' extra years housed, recovery by remissions and deaths, and the community and church programmes by life satisfaction. It comes to about 0.0052 years of healthy life per $1,000, because the help is small next to what even poor US households consume: about $30 of food, goods, money and services a person in a year against consumption of about $10,000, a 0.3% gain on the log scale. Almost two-thirds of the result comes from food, goods, money and services, a fifth from shelter. Every branch is discounted for missing data, since none of the Salvation Army's services has a controlled evaluation: food, goods and money, shelter, placements, recovery, community programmes and worship. The biggest uncertainties are what families would have got without the Salvation Army, how well its counts reflect help delivered, and how poor the clients are.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: The Salvation Army USA, services in the US

summary: Samaritan's Purse, an evangelical relief charity, spent $1.15 billion on its ministries in 2025 (audited accounts): $490 million on Operation Christmas Child's 10.9 million shoebox gifts to children abroad, $295 million on food, water, shelter and health care in crises abroad (Sudan, South Sudan, the DRC, Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, Jamaica), $185 million on US disaster relief and rebuilding, $72 million on mission hospitals and field hospitals, and $103 million on Christian education and other faith work, which the site's scale gives no value beyond its material aid. Every branch is built from spending, Samaritan's Purse's own counts and judged costs, and discounted for missing data; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, the shoeboxes' worth to the children and the cost per person of the relief.

name: Save the Children (UK): advocacy and humanitarian research (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. The two-child limit (about 7%) in the United Kingdom; the Gavi and Nutrition for Growth pledges (about 75%) and Elrha's research (about 20%) over the Gavi-eligible and crisis countries where Save the Children works, weighted towards the largest (Nigeria, the DRC, Ethiopia, Pakistan); a judgment.
summary: Save the Children UK's advocacy and awareness work (£13.5m in 2025) and Elrha, its subsidiary that funds humanitarian research (£11.2m). None publishes a measured result, so each is built from what it won or funds, with ranged judgments, and all four branches are counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: the abolition of the UK's two-child limit on Universal Credit (announced November 2025, from April 2026) as affected families' gain in log income less the payers' loss, the 2026-2030 Gavi pledges and the Nutrition for Growth commitments as the value of the extra aid net of what it displaces, and Elrha's grants as the humanitarian spending improved by studies that change practice. It comes to about 0.13 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.0057 – 0.65), mostly from the Gavi pledges (about seven tenths of the result), then Nutrition for Growth, the two-child limit and Elrha; the result is mostly uncertainty, judgments on what campaigning adds to pledges driving it. The biggest uncertainties are how much of each win the campaigners caused and Save the Children's share of the campaigning.

summary: Save the Children UK's programmes in 2025 (£209m of its £234m charitable spending, mostly passed to Save the Children International, which runs the country work): education in crises (£80m), emergency response (£38m, with the Start Network's pooled fund), health and immunisation (£40m), livelihoods (£20m), child protection (£17m), nutrition (£14m) and a little UK child-poverty work. It counts reach for some projects but not for each line's spending, and publishes no controlled evaluation of its own, so every branch is built from its spending and the research on its kind of work (the median effect of education programmes, mortality in crises, child mortality and immunisation, treatment of severe malnutrition, livelihood trials, mental health in conflict) with wide ranges, and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.22 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.097 – 0.50): a third from education (later earnings), a third from treating severe malnutrition, then emergencies, livelihoods and health; the result is mostly uncertainty, judged costs per child and effects driving it. The biggest uncertainties are what each line costs per child reached and how much of a child's risk of death the health and nutrition work removes.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's childhood cancer, sickle cell and children's influenza burden.
summary: St. Jude spends about $880 million a year on research into childhood cancer and other catastrophic childhood diseases, $720 million of it from its own funds; its cancer research is about a fifth of all childhood cancer research worldwide. For its fiscal year to June 2025 this model credits each of its two branches, cancer (about 70% of the research spending) and the other diseases (sickle cell disease, influenza and basic science, about 30%), with St. Jude's share of what a year of the field's research does to the world's burden of those diseases (the deaths in it valued by age at the site's value of a death, the illness as healthy years), anchored on published returns to medical research. The result is about 0.00068 years of healthy life per $1,000: research pays off only after a long lag, through uptake by others, and the field's progress is shared among all its funders. St. Jude's next dollar counts at 21% of its past average, since it holds about 3.7 years of spending in reserve. Both branches are discounted for missing data, since St. Jude's research has no outcome measure of its own; the result is mostly uncertainty, dominated by judgment (the chance a year's research yields an advance and the share of the burden it averts), and its plausible range is wide (0.00013 to 0.0035).

summary: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis treats about 1,000 new patients a year with childhood cancer and other catastrophic diseases, free to families, supports children's cancer care at partner hospitals in more than 70 countries through St. Jude Global, and trains clinicians and scientists and runs community health programmes. For its fiscal year to June 2025 these come to about 0.0036 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.0005 to 0.03). St. Jude Global, 14% of the cost, brings nearly nine-tenths of the result: partner hospitals in middle-income countries save more children per improvement, but they and their governments carry most of the cost of treatment, so St. Jude's share of the credit is about a fifth, and the gain rests on before-and-after results at a few flagship sites. US care is lower still: about $1 million of St. Jude's own money per new patient buys a few points of survival over the other US centres these children would otherwise attend. Every branch (patient care, St. Jude Global, clinical training, the graduate school, community programmes) is discounted for missing data, since St. Jude publishes no controlled outcome for any of them; training and the community programmes are built from the research on training and on HPV vaccination promotion. The result is mostly uncertainty, above all whether St. Jude Global's support changes survival at partner hospitals at all.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by income group: revenue in low and lower-middle income countries other than India 78% (equally over the nine African countries whose tax authorities the network works with in its 2025 report, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Ethiopia, Zambia, Tanzania, Rwanda and Benin, and Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines), India 9% (valued at GiveWell's lower figure for its government), upper-middle income 10% (Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, South Africa), high income 3% (the UK as a stand-in). summary: The Tax Justice Network, a UK non-profit research and advocacy company founded in 2003 (GBP 2.09 million spent in 2025), proposed the tax-transparency standards now in force worldwide (automatic exchange of tax information, ownership registers, country-by-country reporting) and campaigns for the UN tax convention due in 2027. An average year of its spending since 2003 (from its accounts, about 45% of 2025's in real terms) is counted against its judged 2% share of five years of the revenue those standards raise (the OECD Global Forum's EUR 4 billion a year, 70% in developing countries), and against 6% of a 40% chance that the convention recovers a twentieth of the US$47 billion lower-income countries lose each year, two thirds of that work already done. Revenue in low and lower-middle income countries is valued as GiveWell values government spending there (about 1.5 times cash, India's a quarter of that), elsewhere as money spread over citizens' consumption, both net of what the tax costs the rich who pay it. summary: Ubongo makes educational cartoons for TV, radio and online in Africa: Akili and Me for children of 3-6 (early literacy, numeracy, English, emotions) and Ubongo Kids for 7-14 (maths and science), broadcast free in about 22 countries; its US arm spent 7.2 million dollars in 2024 and Ubongo counts 42 million households reached a month, so the cost per child is a few cents. Children in poor countries who watch Sesame Street's local versions at home learn about a fifth of a standard deviation more than those who don't (Ubongo's own trials point the same way), and we value that as higher adult earnings after cutting it for occasional viewers, survey and small-study bias, repeat years of viewing and fade-out. That gives about 52 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, but the result is mostly uncertainty (plausible range about 8 to 270): the size of the home-viewing effect, how much of it lasts into adult earnings, and whether the audience counts are right drive it. The whole programme is discounted for missing data, as no study measures Ubongo's home audience in standard deviations.

name: United Way (US network, charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US United Way network.
summary: The US United Way network (about 1,100 local United Ways and their national office, United Way Worldwide) raises money, mostly through workplace campaigns, and spends it on grants to local agencies (about 58% of its programme spending), the 211 helplines it runs or funds, free tax filing and programmes of its own. All of it is modelled, for the network's fiscal year to June 2025 ($3.5 billion spent), in five branches: basic-needs grants valued near cash; other grants and United Way's own services (about 80% of programme spending, including the cost of running the grants) built from the US research on programmes of their kind, children's tutoring, mentoring, early learning and after-school programmes valued by the adult earnings the trials imply, job training and coaching by earnings gained, health services at what low-income recipients would pay for them; 211 by the help callers find that they wouldn't have found otherwise; and tax help by fees saved and credits that would have gone unclaimed. Every branch is discounted for missing data, since United Way measures none of these outcomes itself. The result, about 0.011 years of healthy life per $1,000, is low because the help goes to people in the US who consume around $23,000 a year (those getting food and rent help about $10,000): on the site's log-income scale a dollar does a thirteenth to a thirtieth of what it does for a household living on about $2 a day, and United Way's money buys services at US prices. About half the result is the children's and youth programmes' lifelong earnings, so the discount rate, how much the programmes raise earnings and what they cost drive it, with the missing-data and income-to-health sliders.

beneficiaries_note: Our build: USA for UNHCR's 2025 grants by region (Form 990 Schedule F, cash and goods: Sub-Saharan Africa $19.7M, Middle East and North Africa $12.1M, South Asia $8.2M, Europe $6.0M, South America $3.9M, Russia and neighbouring states $2.2M, North America $1.1M, East Asia and the Pacific $0.6M) spread over the largest UNHCR refugee operations in each region (Sudan's neighbours and Sudan, Uganda, Ethiopia, the DRC; Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Egypt; Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Pakistan; Ukraine and Moldova; Colombia, Peru, Ecuador; Mexico; Myanmar). summary: USA for UNHCR raises money in the United States for UNHCR, the UN refugee agency: in 2025 it spent $95.5 million, of which $44.3 million went as cash grants to UNHCR's operations (most to Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and South Asia), $10.6 million of donated clothes, hygiene kits, software and transport passed on (the donors' resources, so credited by share rather than costed), and $8.2 million on awareness work; fundraising took $26.6 million, so each cash dollar granted costs about $1.61 of donations. The grants are valued as UNHCR's 2025 programme mix (its audited impact areas, split further by judgment): cash, relief items and shelter (excess deaths averted and goods on the site's log-income scale), health care in camps (deaths averted), registration, documents and protection services (consumption and mental-health gains), education, livelihoods, and resettlement and returns. Neither USA for UNHCR nor UNHCR counts who this money reached, so every branch rests on judged costs per person and the research on its kind of work and is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.060 years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range 0.030 – 0.15: the result is mostly uncertainty), mostly because about 38% of each cash dollar pays for fundraising and management in the US and a quarter of UNHCR's for its own support costs; the biggest uncertainties are the missing-data discount, how many refugees' papers bring them rights, and how poor the people reached are.

name: Village Enterprise: poverty graduation in East Africa (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults (households × first-year gain × evidence and missing-data steps): Uganda's core program, DREAMS and SPRINT 32%, Kenya 28%, Ethiopia's DREAMS camps 25%, Rwanda 12%, Tanzania's DREAMS 3%; the government-adoption row, under 1%, left out.
summary: Village Enterprise runs a one-year poverty graduation program for the poorest rural households in Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Tanzania: business training, seed grants to groups of three entrepreneurs, mentoring and savings groups, a quarter of the households in DREAMS, its program for refugee settlements with Mercy Corps in Uganda and Ethiopia and through local organisations in Tanzania. Against its fiscal year 2025 spending (US$21.0M with overhead, 47,505 households), two randomized trials of the program itself (consumption 7.3% higher in Kenya, 3.6% in Uganda, 17% in DREAMS and 13% for its refugees, among all households offered the program) give about 3.8 years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainty is how long the consumption gain lasts: the trials followed households for at most 2.5 years after the program, and the model assumes a gain fading 5% a year for 8 years (3 to 12). Tanzania's DREAMS households, the SPRINT digital pilot and governments' adoption of the model, which no trial has tested, are discounted for missing data.

name: World Central Kitchen: emergency meals (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by branch (Gaza 72%, crises in poorer countries 28%, rich-country disasters under 1%), the poorer-country branch split by its places' spending weights from the Form 990's Schedule F times their log gains (Haiti, Jamaica, Ukraine standing in for the middle-income places, Myanmar for East Asia); the rich-country branch at the US.
summary: World Central Kitchen cooks and delivers hot meals after disasters and in wars; in 2025 it spent 372.5 million dollars on this, its only programme, and served 130 to 179 million meals, about 70% of them in Gaza, the rest mostly in Haiti, Ukraine, Jamaica, Myanmar and US and European disasters. The model values the meals as food on the site's log-income scale and, in Gaza and poorer countries' crises, as a share of the excess deaths from hunger they avert, in three branches split by the Form 990's regions: about 0.12 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars at the defaults, over 70% of it from Gaza. Each branch's food is valued from its share of the food bill, over the months people were fed. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the food in Gaza others would have brought in through the same crossings, and how little people there had without it; no study measures what the meals do, so every branch is discounted for missing data.

name: Wounded Warrior Project: mental health (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Wounded Warrior Project's mental health programmes for US veterans.
summary: Wounded Warrior Project pays four academic medical centres (Warrior Care Network) to run two- and three-week intensive PTSD programmes and outpatient therapy for post-9/11 veterans, and runs its own counselling, Project Odyssey retreats, WWP Talk calls and case coordination. Our model of its mental health spending in fiscal 2025 ($98.7M; 1,286 veterans in the intensive programmes, about 12,000 others) takes the effect from trials of trauma-focused therapy in military personnel (about 0.85 SD on depression measures at the end of treatment, fading over about four years) and adds the suicides it averts; it comes to about 0.0016 years of healthy life per $1,000, low because each person costs about $11,000 and a WELLBY is worth a fifteenth of a healthy year at the site's rate. The therapy and support branches are discounted for missing data (no controlled evaluation of WWP's outpatient therapy, counselling, Project Odyssey or WWP Talk); the intensive programmes are measured. The biggest uncertainties are how long the effect lasts and how much of it the VA's own PTSD care would have given anyway.

name: Wounded Warrior Project (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Wounded Warrior Project's programmes for post-9/11 veterans in the US (mental health has its own model).
summary: Wounded Warrior Project serves post-9/11 veterans injured in service and their families in the United States: it wins VA disability benefits for them, places them in jobs, gives emergency grants and financial counselling, runs social and fitness events, pays for in-home care for the most severely injured, funds other veteran charities and lobbies Congress. Our model of every programme but mental health in fiscal 2025 ($175.9M of $274.6M programme spending; mental health is wounded-warrior-project-charityevals-mental-health) values the benefits won, jobs, grants and care on the site's log-income scale, the benefits net of what they cost taxpayers, the events by life satisfaction, and the Major Richard Star Act's chance of passing; it comes to about 0.0064 years of healthy life per $1,000, low because the help goes to US households that already consume about $27,000 a person, and most VA awards it helps win would have come through another free representative or later. About four-fifths of the result is the benefits service ($263.7M of awards in WWP's own unexplained 'economic impact' figure), net of what the awards cost taxpayers, with credit shared with the VA's own cost of deciding the claims. Every branch but the emergency grants is discounted for missing data: benefits, Warriors to Work, financial readiness, connection, physical health, the Independence Program, community partnerships and advocacy. The biggest uncertainties are how many years of payments an award adds over what veterans would have won anyway and how far below average the veterans' consumption is; with every judgment at its ends the result spans over a thousandfold, so it is mostly uncertainty.
